title: Rank-size analysis of optimal portfolio weights with a reverse-engineering application
summary: This paper investigates the shape of optimal portfolio weights using rank-size analysis. We consider four portfolio selection models: Global Minimum-Variance (GMV), minimum-CVaR, Risk Parity (RP), and the Most Diversified Portfolio (MDP). For each model, we fit seven rank-size specifications to the sorted portfolio weights generated over rolling windows. To compare the fitted specifications, we combine standard goodness-of-fit measures with Cumulative Second-order $\varepsilon$-Stochastic Dominance, an $\varepsilon$-parameterized generalization of Second-order Stochastic Dominance that quantifies the extent to which the exact dominance conditions are satisfied or violated. Empirically applied to major equity indices, this approach provides a systematic criterion for identifying the optimal functional form across diverse market compositions. Furthermore, we address the inverse problem of identifying the generating model from the observed weight structure. We use the calibrated rank-size parameters as inputs to a Random Forest classifier, evaluated by a blocked cross-validation that accounts for the overlap between estimation windows. The parameters separate minimum-risk from risk-diversification strategies and identify the RP and MDP portfolios, whereas the GMV and minimum-CVaR portfolios are difficult to distinguish. These results indicate that rank-size parameters provide a compact and informative description of portfolio allocation geometries.
core_methodology: The paper employs rank-size analysis to evaluate optimal portfolio weights across four portfolio selection models (GMV, minimum-CVaR, RP, MDP). It fits seven rank-size specifications to sorted weights over rolling windows and uses a combination of goodness-of-fit measures and ε-Stochastic Dominance for comparison. The inverse problem is addressed using a Random Forest classifier to identify the generating model from observed weight structures.
data_sources: Major equity indices (specific indices not mentioned in abstract but implied to be standard market benchmarks).
alpha_potential: The methodology provides a systematic way to identify optimal functional forms for portfolio weights across different market conditions, which can enhance portfolio construction and risk management. The ability to reverse-engineer the generating model from weight structures could offer insights into market dynamics and improve tactical asset allocation.
title_cn: 最优投资组合权重的秩-规模分析及逆向工程应用
summary_cn: 本文通过秩-规模分析研究了四种投资组合模型（全局最小方差、最小CVaR、风险平价和最分散组合）的权重结构。结合拟合优度指标和ε-随机占优方法，系统评估了不同市场条件下最优权重形式。通过随机森林分类器逆向推导生成模型，为组合构建和风险管理提供了实用工具，可用于优化战术资产配置。

title: Cleaning correlation matrices with external information: the Maximum Variance estimator
summary: Rotationally invariant estimators clean the eigenvalues of an empirical correlation matrix but keep its noisy eigenvectors. We study an estimator that corrects the eigenvectors by using external information, namely a partition of the assets into groups such as asset classes or regions. The Maximum Variance (MaxVar) estimator restricts the leading eigenvectors to linear combinations of the maximum-variance portfolios of the groups and replaces the rest of the spectrum by a single eigenvalue. It is a factor model with about n parameters instead of n2/2, and it is positive de nite even when the number of observations is smaller than the number of assets n. We apply it to the correlation matrix of 47 futures on stock indices, bonds and currencies, with the three asset classes as groups. In an illustrative Monte Carlo test, in which the reference matrix has the structure assumed by the estimator, the distance to the reference is reduced by one third with respect to the empirical matrix, against less than 10% for the rotationally invariant estimator. The decisive test is the performance of a portfolio on real data: over 1993-2018, the Sharpe ratio of the risk parity portfolio, which involves the inverse of the matrix, is 1.28 with the MaxVar estimator, 1.24 with the rotationally invariant estimator and 1.17 with the empirical matrix, and the advantage increases when the estimation window is shortened.
core_methodology: The paper introduces the Maximum Variance (MaxVar) estimator, which corrects eigenvectors in a correlation matrix by leveraging external grouping information (e.g., asset classes or regions). It restricts leading eigenvectors to linear combinations of maximum-variance portfolios of the groups and replaces the remaining spectrum with a single eigenvalue, effectively creating a factor model with reduced parameters.
data_sources: The study uses empirical correlation matrices from 47 futures on stock indices, bonds, and currencies, categorized into three asset classes.
alpha_potential: The MaxVar estimator demonstrates improved performance in portfolio optimization, particularly for risk parity portfolios, by enhancing the accuracy of correlation matrices and their inverses. This leads to higher Sharpe ratios compared to traditional rotationally invariant estimators, especially in short estimation windows.
title_cn: 利用外部信息清洗相关矩阵：最大方差估计器
summary_cn: 该论文提出的最大方差估计器通过利用资产分组信息（如资产类别或地区）优化相关矩阵的特征向量，显著提升了投资组合优化效果。在实际应用中，该方法在风险平价组合中表现优异，夏普比率优于传统旋转不变估计器，特别是在短估计窗口内。

title: One Token, Many Lessons: Sliding-Window Attention within Gated Delta Networks
summary: Linear attention compresses historical context into a fixed-size recurrent state, reducing the computational and memory costs of long-sequence modeling. From the perspective of test-time regression (TTR), the state matrix can be viewed as an online-learned regression model, where keys and values serve as inputs and targets respectively, and queries are used to read from the model. From this perspective, the effectiveness of state learning depends not only on the update rule but also on how the key-value learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. While existing work has largely focused on how the state is updated and organized, we investigate how the learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. To this end, we propose Sliding-Window Gated DeltaNet (SWGDN), which replaces short convolutions in Delta-Rule linear attention with sliding-window attention to perform content-dependent local aggregation of projected queries, keys, and values. Our experiments show that SWGDN makes the key-value pairs used in consecutive updates more similar in both GDN2 and KDA. In SWGDN, carrying information from the same token across updates can help the recurrent state reinforce a previously learned association. The local mixing strategy can be incorporated into any Delta-Rule-based linear attention architecture without changing its state update equations or chunkwise parallel algorithms. We apply this strategy to two Delta-Rule variants, GDN2 and KDA, and experimental results demonstrate that SWGDN outperforms the original Delta-Rule baseline across multiple benchmarks.
core_methodology: The paper introduces Sliding-Window Gated DeltaNet (SWGDN), which enhances linear attention mechanisms by using sliding-window attention for content-dependent local aggregation of queries, keys, and values. This improves the similarity of key-value pairs in consecutive updates, reinforcing learned associations in the recurrent state.
data_sources: The abstract does not specify particular data sources, but the methodology is general and could be applied to any sequential data, including financial time series.
alpha_potential: The methodology could be adapted to improve the modeling of financial time series, particularly in scenarios where capturing long-term dependencies and reinforcing learned patterns is crucial. This could be relevant for predictive modeling in trading strategies.

title: Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge to Guide Continual Learning
summary: The goal of continual learning (CL) is to adapt to new data (plasticity) while retaining the knowledge acquired from old data (stability). Existing methods are explicitly designed to focus on balancing stability and plasticity to mitigate the challenge of catastrophic forgetting while promoting learning. However, the impact of order and nature of samples from the new data that the network is trained on remains an under explored factor. We argue that a CL algorithm should have the ability to rank incoming samples in terms of their relationship with prior data and their effect on the learning process. In this work, we investigate if scoring and prioritizing incoming data based on their semantic relationships with the model's current knowledge can benefit CL. We propose SACK, short for Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge, a plug and play technique for continual learning methods. SACK dissects categorical knowledge of the model into fine-grained concepts, computes the relationships between previously learned concepts and new concepts in each experience, and uses this relationship knowledge for prioritizing new samples. Experiments across several types of CL methods (regularization, replay, and prompt based) in class incremental and task incremental settings demonstrate that integration of SACK not only improves accuracy and reduces forgetting but also handles long tail distribution, helps focus on semantically interpretable regions, and yields better calibrated and robust models compared to prior approaches.
core_methodology: Proposes SACK, a plug-and-play technique for continual learning that scores and prioritizes incoming data based on semantic relationships with prior knowledge to improve stability and plasticity in learning.
data_sources: Not explicitly mentioned, but likely involves categorical or labeled datasets for training and testing the CL methods.
alpha_potential: Potential to improve adaptive models in trading by better handling new market regimes or data shifts without forgetting prior knowledge, useful for dynamic asset allocation or strategy adaptation.
title_cn: 顺序获取概念知识以指导持续学习
summary_cn: 该论文提出的SACK技术通过语义关系评分和优先级排序新数据，提升持续学习方法的稳定性和可塑性。在量化交易中，可用于动态调整投资策略，适应市场变化而不遗忘历史数据，具有增强模型鲁棒性和适应性的潜力。

title: Yet Another Concept Drift Benchmark? A Principled Framework for Evaluating Drift Detectors
summary: Concept drift detection is a fundamental component of data stream learning, yet its empirical evaluation remains based on loosely defined protocols, ambiguous alarm semantics, and inconsistent metrics. We propose a principled benchmark grounded in an explicit formulation of drift observability and alarm semantics. Our framework introduces finite detection windows and repeated alarms, enabling a clear separation between detection accuracy, timeliness, and stability, and employs a reproducible observer to provide a controlled and interpretable performance signal. Building on this formulation, we define normalized evaluation metrics and a composite score addressing limitations of existing measures. We validate the framework through a large-scale stress-testing evaluation of 10 detectors across 9 learner configurations and 16 datasets.
core_methodology: A principled framework for evaluating concept drift detectors with explicit formulation of drift observability, alarm semantics, and controlled performance signals.
data_sources: 16 datasets from data stream learning context (specific datasets not disclosed in abstract).
alpha_potential: The framework could potentially improve robustness of ML models in trading strategies by better detecting regime changes or market condition shifts, though direct financial application requires adaptation.
title_cn: 又一个概念漂移基准？基于原则的漂移检测器评估框架
summary_cn: 本文提出了一种结构化的概念漂移检测评估方法，通过明确定义检测窗口和警报机制来分离准确性、时效性和稳定性指标。在量化交易中，该框架可帮助优化算法对市场状态变化的响应能力，但需针对金融时间序列特点进行改进。

title: Learning to Reason in Real-Time
summary: AI agents that operate in the real world must reason correctly and on-time, yet they currently do not account for how time should alter their reasoning. Modern agents learn to do tasks in environments that are entirely synchronous: where the world waits for the agent to act before changing. A real-time environment, by contrast, changes independent of the agent. Existing approaches try to bridge this gap by imposing a ratio of thinking to acting. However, for an agent to succeed in real-time it must learn to act quickly when delay is costly and to reason longer when the benefit outweighs the missed opportunities. To this end, we introduce real-time reasoning training (RRT) as the class of training techniques for real-time reasoning agents. We develop three standard RRT techniques: (1) using real-time data, (2) decoupling acting and observing, and (3) curriculum learning in time. Together, these simple techniques substantially outperform strong baselines. Across time pressures, we outperform the strongest non-RRT baseline by an average of 33% reward on in-distribution and 55% reward on out-of-distribution tasks in two real-time environments: Frogger and Snake. These results demonstrate that we can teach agents to balance reasoning and responsiveness under real-time constraints, and that RRT opens a broad, new set of capabilities for real-time agents.
core_methodology: Real-time reasoning training (RRT) techniques that teach agents to balance reasoning speed and responsiveness under time constraints, using methods like real-time data, decoupling acting and observing, and curriculum learning in time.
data_sources: Not explicitly mentioned, but implies real-time environmental data (e.g., financial tick data could be analogous to the Frogger/Snake environments used).
alpha_potential: Potential for improving high-frequency trading (HFT) or algorithmic execution strategies where latency-critical decisions must balance computation time against market opportunity costs. Could help optimize trade-offs between signal refinement and execution speed.
title_cn: 实时推理学习
summary_cn: 本文提出的实时推理训练（RRT）技术通过分离观察与决策、时间课程学习等方法，使AI代理能在时间压力下动态平衡思考深度与响应速度。对于量化交易，该框架可优化高频交易系统的延迟-信号质量权衡，尤其在基于强化学习的执行算法中具有应用潜力。

title: State Space Attention: Learning Context-Dependent Memory Retention
summary: Standard attention's key-value cache grows linearly with context length. Bounding it raises the question of what a sequence model should retain for long-context reasoning. We argue this choice should be learned, and introduce State Space Attention (SSA), which learns to keep a bounded set of past representations and reads them with standard attention. A learned scorer rescores every chunk against newly arriving context and the rest of memory. A fixed-context Transformer is then the special case that always keeps the most recent tokens. We train the scorer and reader jointly, either moving gradually from a differentiable soft weighting of memories to hard retention, or with hard retention from the start. To produce signal for the scorer, we generate supervised samples during training, a technique we call recovery. We compare SSA with recurrent models, bounded-memory attention methods, and full-attention Transformers across retrieval, variable tracking, multi-hop reasoning, and language modeling. On our retrieval and reasoning benchmarks, SSA matches or comes within a few points of full attention on most tasks, far outperforms a Transformer with the same readable budget on every long-context retrieval task we evaluate, and matches or outperforms one with about 4 times that budget, while using constant inference memory. The largest remaining gap to full attention at small language model scale is on RULER. SSA makes a fixed number of tokens useful over a longer context, and since it reads memory with standard attention, we propose that it can be stacked with KV cache eviction methods. We also pretrain and post-train 400M-parameter models and measure how SSA's training and inference costs scale with context length and model size. Together, these experiments examine the capabilities and limitations of learned memory retention for long-context sequence modeling.
core_methodology: State Space Attention (SSA) learns to retain a bounded set of past representations for long-context reasoning, using a learned scorer to rescore past chunks against new context.
data_sources: Benchmarks include retrieval, variable tracking, multi-hop reasoning, and language modeling, though specific financial datasets are not mentioned.
alpha_potential: Potential applications in processing long-context financial time series data or enhancing sequence models used in algorithmic trading, though direct trading applications are not demonstrated.

title: Physics-Informed Learning for Multiplayer Differential Games
summary: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $\varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.
core_methodology: Physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme for approximating viscosity solutions in N-player adversarial differential games.
data_sources: Simulated environments (e.g., pursuit-evasion scenarios) rather than real-world financial data.
alpha_potential: Potential application in modeling strategic interactions in market making or high-frequency trading scenarios where multiple agents interact competitively. However, requires adaptation to financial data.
title_cn: 物理信息学习在多玩家微分博弈中的应用
summary_cn: 该论文提出了一种基于物理信息神经网络的策略迭代方法，用于解决高维多玩家对抗微分博弈中的反馈策略计算问题。在量化交易中，该方法可能适用于模拟市场中性策略或多代理竞争环境中的动态博弈，但尚未直接应用于金融市场数据。

title: CovNovBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models under Covariate Novelty
summary: Covariate-aware time-series foundation models (TSFMs) condition their forecasts on additional input variables, called covariates, that are supplied over the future horizon. This capability makes them appealing for interventional forecasting, in which a target is predicted under a planned action such as a new product pricing policy or a new patient treatment schedule. We refer to covariates that encode such actions as treatment covariates. Current covariate-aware TSFMs, however, are trained on observed patterns, and their behavior is unclear when future treatment covariates fall outside the range seen in the history. Examples include a numerical treatment that leaves its historical range and a categorical treatment that takes a previously unseen policy. We call this practically common setting covariate novelty, and note that it is not systematically represented in existing benchmarks. We introduce an operational definition of covariate novelty and use it to construct CovNovBench, a benchmark of 88,476 evaluation series generated or filtered from four simulator-based and real-world datasets. The benchmark spans categorical and numerical treatment covariates as well as stable and trending targets. We evaluate six covariate-aware TSFMs zero-shot using point and directional accuracy metrics. No model is consistently reliable in our benchmark: point error almost always increases under covariate novelty, directional performance changes non-uniformly, and the best observed model varies across datasets and metrics. CovNovBench provides a systematic testbed for developing TSFMs that forecast more reliably under covariate novelty.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a benchmark (CovNovBench) to evaluate time series foundation models (TSFMs) under covariate novelty conditions, where future treatment covariates fall outside historical ranges. The methodology involves creating systematic tests for model reliability under these conditions using both point and directional accuracy metrics.
data_sources: The benchmark uses 88,476 evaluation series generated or filtered from four simulator-based and real-world datasets, covering categorical and numerical treatment covariates as well as stable and trending targets.
alpha_potential: The paper highlights the potential for improved forecasting under novel conditions, which could be valuable for trading strategies that rely on predictive models for scenarios like sudden market regime changes or unconventional policy interventions. However, the direct application to financial markets is not explicitly demonstrated.
title_cn: CovNovBench：评估协变量新颖性下的时间序列基础模型的基准
summary_cn: 该论文提出了一个基准（CovNovBench），用于评估在协变量新颖性（即未来协变量超出历史范围）条件下时间序列基础模型（TSFMs）的可靠性。通过对四类数据集（包括模拟和真实数据）的测试，发现现有模型在协变量新颖性条件下的表现不稳定。这一研究对量化交易中应对市场突变或政策干预等非常规情境的预测模型改进具有潜在价值，但需进一步验证其在金融市场的直接应用。

title: Normalizing Flows are Capable World Models
summary: A world model lets an agent anticipate the consequences of its actions and use imagined futures to make decisions. We introduce Normalizing-Flow World Model (NFWM), which pairs an invertible observation encoder with an action-conditioned probabilistic predictor. Because the encoder is invertible, the predicted distribution over latent states defines a distribution over future observations. Maximizing the exact conditional likelihood of those observations therefore trains the representation and dynamics jointly. An agent can plan directly in the learned latent space and decode sampled trajectories to inspect possible futures. On Teleport, these samples capture the two possible outcomes of the same action. In Flappy Bird, a world model trained by likelihood alone supports reward-based planning that reaches 100 pipes in all ten evaluated games. For goal-conditioned control, an auxiliary inverse-dynamics objective shapes the coordinates used to compare predicted states with a goal. On LIBERO, NFWM uses this distance to select successful action sequences more often than LeWM and SMWM. In Atari Boxing, training on imagined trajectories improves a policy beyond its behavior-cloned initialization. Together, these results establish normalizing flows as capable world models.
core_methodology: The paper introduces Normalizing-Flow World Model (NFWM), which uses an invertible observation encoder and an action-conditioned probabilistic predictor to model future states and observations. This approach allows for exact conditional likelihood maximization and supports planning in the learned latent space.
data_sources: The paper does not explicitly mention financial data sources but focuses on general world modeling applicable to various environments (e.g., Teleport, Flappy Bird, LIBERO, Atari Boxing).
alpha_potential: NFWM could be adapted to financial markets for scenario generation, risk assessment, and strategic planning by modeling potential future market states conditioned on different actions or events. The exact likelihood maximization could help in capturing complex market dynamics.
title_cn: 规范化流作为能力世界模型
summary_cn: 该论文提出的规范化流世界模型（NFWM）通过可逆观察编码器和动作条件概率预测器，能够精确建模未来状态和观察结果。在金融交易中，该方法可以用于市场情景生成和风险管理，通过潜在空间规划来预测不同市场行为的影响。

title: Random Voronoi Networks
summary: Nearest-neighbor methods are local, simple, and interpretable, but their non-parametric form makes them memory-intensive, expensive at inference, and difficult to integrate into differentiable neural architectures. We introduce Random Voronoi Networks (RVNs), a family of structured three-layer MLPs that express nearest-neighbor geometry through sampled Voronoi comparisons. The first layer computes Random Voronoi Features (RVF) from affine pairwise separators between selected training samples, the second layer aggregates these comparisons into Voronoi cells or top-k neighborhood scores, and the readout layer produces classification or regression predictions. We show that, when all samples and pairwise comparisons are included, step RVNs recover exact Euclidean k-NN, while ReLU RVNs provide a violation-score realization for 1-NN that can be relaxed into a differentiable soft weighting. Subsampling yields approximate RVNs with explicit control over the number of cells and features. We study several unsupervised sampling methods that trade off random coverage, directional diversity, coordinate sparsity, and empirical feature variance. Empirically, RVFs produce a highly effective data encoding strategy, providing performance boosts to downstream methods ranging from linear to modern tabular deep learning models. Finally, we showcase that RVF provides an interpretable feature map due to its k-NN based construction and ties to pairwise local directions. These results position our Random Voronoi formulation as a bridge between nearest-neighbor rules, random features, and modern tabular models.
core_methodology: Random Voronoi Networks (RVNs) use structured three-layer MLPs to approximate nearest-neighbor methods through sampled Voronoi comparisons, providing a differentiable and memory-efficient alternative to traditional k-NN approaches.
data_sources: The paper does not specify financial data sources, but the methodology can be applied to tabular financial data such as stock prices, returns, or other market indicators.
alpha_potential: RVNs could potentially capture local patterns in financial data, such as momentum or mean-reversion signals, by leveraging their interpretable and efficient nearest-neighbor-like structure. The method's ability to handle high-dimensional data and provide differentiable outputs may enhance feature engineering and model interpretability in trading strategies.

title: DLaR: Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Latent reasoning enables LLMs to operate in continuous embedding space, yet existing methods suffer from deterministic inference that precludes exploration of diverse reasoning paths. While recent approaches inject stochasticity to restore exploration, we identify two fundamental limitations: \textit{uniform stochasticity} across all steps is suboptimal, and unconstrained perturbations disrupt reasoning coherence. We propose Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning (DLaR), a framework with two complementary mechanisms that operate at different temporal granularities within the GRPO reinforcement learning framework. At the token level, Adaptive Stochasticity Modulation (ASM) dynamically adjusts perturbation intensity at each latent step based on a confidence-entropy fusion signal, increasing exploration when the model is uncertain and preserving stability when confident. At the training level, Training-Aware Stochasticity Tuning (TAST) progressively decays the base stochasticity level following a curriculum schedule. Through this dual-level design, DLaR establishes a hierarchical exploration-exploitation strategy that operates at both token and training levels. Extensive experiments on four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that DLaR achieves the highest average performance across model scales, reaching 27.9%/50.6% Pass@1/Pass@8 on Llama-3.2-1B and 46.8%/68.2% on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Code: \href{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}.
core_methodology: Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning (DLaR) adapts perturbation intensity at each latent step based on a confidence-entropy fusion signal and progressively decays base stochasticity level during training.
data_sources: Mathematical reasoning benchmarks (in-distribution and out-of-distribution).
alpha_potential: The adaptive stochasticity modulation could potentially improve decision-making in uncertain market conditions, enhancing the robustness of LLM-based trading strategies. However, its direct application to financial datasets would require significant adaptation.
title_cn: DLaR：用于大型语言模型潜在推理的动态随机性控制
summary_cn: DLaR框架通过双重机制动态调整推理过程中的随机性，提升模型在数学推理任务上的表现。此方法若应用于金融市场，可能提高交易策略在不确定性环境下的适应性和稳健性。

title: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2: Understanding and Mitigating Recurrent State Instability
summary: Linear attention offers an efficient solution for long-sequence modeling via linear complexity and fixed-size recurrent states. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) introduces independent channel-wise control over erasure and writing, enhancing state-update expressiveness and in-context retrieval, yet it suffers from training failures during long-context training. We trace these failures to the asymmetry between reading and modification directions during erasure, which yields non-normal erase operators whose directional gains accumulate across tokens, triggering exponential state growth even without new writes. To resolve this, we propose \model{}, employing symmetric erasure to ensure non-expansive state propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to preserve writing flexibility. Theoretically, we establish an $O(\sqrt{T})$ upper bound on recurrent state growth while retaining chunkwise parallel computation. Experiments on ~1.6B parameter models show that \model{} achieves stable training alongside improved long-context retrieval. Compared to GDN-2, it boosts the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in the recurrent setting and average accuracy across nine downstream tasks by 0.62 points in the hybrid setting.
core_methodology: The paper proposes Stable Gated DeltaNet-2, a modified linear attention mechanism with symmetric erasure and decay-regulated residual writing to address recurrent state instability in long-context training. This ensures non-expansive state propagation and stable training while retaining parallel computation capabilities.
data_sources: Not explicitly mentioned, but the methodology is applicable to any sequential data, which could include financial time series or order book data.
alpha_potential: The improved stability and long-context retrieval could enhance time-series forecasting models in trading by better capturing long-range dependencies in market data, potentially leading to more accurate predictions of price movements or market regime shifts.
title_cn: 稳定门控DeltaNet-2：理解与缓解循环状态不稳定性
summary_cn: 该论文提出了一种改进的线性注意力机制，通过对称擦除和衰减调节的残差写入解决长上下文训练中的循环状态不稳定问题。该方法可应用于金融时间序列建模，提升长程依赖捕捉能力，对市场趋势预测和交易信号生成具有潜在价值。

title: Text-Conditioned Low-Rank Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models for Multimodal Forecasting
summary: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) provide transferable numerical forecasting priors. However, forecast-relevant information may be conveyed in text without being reflected in the observed series. Many multimodal forecasting methods integrate such context through model inputs or intermediate representations. We investigate a complementary mechanism: text-conditioned parameter adaptation. We propose Context-to-LoRA for Time Series (C2LoRA-TS), which encodes text and generates temporary Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) updates for selected weight matrices of a frozen TSFM. Both the numerical backbone and text encoder remain frozen, and the method exactly recovers the frozen TSFM output when context is absent. Evaluated on Time-MMD across nine domains and three TSFM architectures, C2LoRA-TS achieves lower aggregate forecasting error than the frozen-TSFM and Static LoRA baselines for every architecture and seed. Replacing the instance-specific text with a single globally fixed context degrades performance for every architecture. These results support text-conditioned parameter generation as a viable strategy for multimodal forecasting with frozen TSFMs.
core_methodology: The paper introduces C2LoRA-TS, a method for text-conditioned parameter adaptation in time-series foundation models (TSFMs) using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to integrate text context for improved multimodal forecasting.
data_sources: The method is evaluated on Time-MMD across nine domains, suggesting it uses multimodal data combining numerical time-series and textual context.
alpha_potential: The approach could potentially enhance forecasting models by incorporating textual context that isn't reflected in numerical data alone, which might be useful for sentiment analysis or news-driven trading strategies.

title: Kant-Q: A Q-Learning Algorithm for Kantian Equilibrium in Symmetric Markov Games
summary: AI agents increasingly interact with one another, and many of these interactions are mixed-motive games, which have posed a persistent challenge for learning algorithms. Most multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms are designed to reach Nash equilibria, yet in many such games these equilibria are Pareto-inefficient. We instead study Kantian equilibria, an economic solution concept in which each agent plays the action it would want all agents to adopt. In symmetric games, this corresponds to an optimal common policy. We propose Kant-Q, a Q-learning algorithm in which each agent learns action profiles where all agents play the same action. Each update is then a sample from a single-agent MDP, so Kant-Q inherits the convergence guarantees of standard Q-learning. We show that every symmetric Markov game has a pure Kantian equilibrium. We also prove that all agents' Q-tables converge to the same limit, whose greedy policy is such an equilibrium, and that greedy play converges whenever the optimal common action is unique at every state. We further show that in a subclass of symmetric monotone games, the Kantian equilibrium is Pareto-efficient among pure strategy profiles and strictly individually rational. Empirically, on the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma and the GovSim fishery with up to 200 agents, Kant-Q learns the Kantian equilibrium, while the baselines underperform. Since copies of the same AI system naturally face one another in symmetric games, these results suggest universalization as a design principle for cooperative AI-AI interaction.
core_methodology: A Q-learning algorithm designed to find Kantian equilibria in symmetric Markov games, focusing on cooperative play among multiple agents.
data_sources: The paper uses synthetic and canonical game theory scenarios (e.g., iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, GovSim fishery) rather than financial market data.
alpha_potential: Potential applications in cooperative multi-agent trading environments where multiple algorithmic traders interact, seeking Pareto-efficient strategies to avoid Nash equilibrium pitfalls.
title_cn: Kant-Q：对称马尔可夫博弈中康德均衡的Q学习算法

title: Do We Still Need Reinforcement Learning When We Can Read the World Model?
summary: Reinforcement learning has achieved remarkable success in sequential decision-making, but learning effective policies often requires substantial interaction experience. Model-based reinforcement learning alleviates this dependence by leveraging world models, which are typically used to support planning or policy optimization. In this paper, we investigate an alternative paradigm in which autonomous LLM-based coding agents directly synthesize control policies by reasoning over readable world models. By examining environment source code, these agents translate environmental knowledge into executable decision rules and iteratively refine their policies using online feedback or offline data, without task-specific RL training. Experiments across diverse decision-making benchmarks show that synthesized policies match or outperform conventional RL methods while requiring substantially less experience. Further analyses reveal interpretable decision rules and how they evolve through feedback-driven refinement. Comparisons with policies generated without source code access and experiments under challenging conditions further demonstrate the benefits of readable world models. These findings suggest that direct policy synthesis can reduce reliance on trial and error, challenging the necessity of task-specific RL training.
core_methodology: Autonomous LLM-based coding agents synthesize control policies by reasoning over readable world models (environment source code), iteratively refining policies using feedback without traditional RL training.
data_sources: Environment source code (readable world models) and feedback from benchmarks or offline data.
alpha_potential: Potential to create interpretable decision rules for trading strategies, reducing reliance on trial-and-error RL training and accelerating strategy development.

title: Provably Efficient Concave Utility Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation
summary: Concave utility reinforcement learning (CURL) unifies a diverse range of problems, including standard reinforcement learning (RL), imitation learning, and maximum entropy exploration. Unlike standard RL, CURL generally requires estimating high-dimensional state-action occupancy measures. Consequently, existing methods for CURL either sidestep the exploration problem, are restricted to the tabular setting, or lack computationally efficient policy optimization. To address this, we study CURL in finite-horizon episodic bilinear MDPs, where the transition model admits a low-dimensional representation in known feature spaces. We use the bilinear structure to efficiently estimate occupancy measures via low-dimensional feature expectations, and propose a model-based optimistic concave utility policy optimization (OCUPO) framework. We first instantiate OCUPO in the on-policy setting, where each iteration uses independent trajectories to estimate the concave utility policy gradient, and prove an $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ sample complexity. To improve sample efficiency, we then instantiate OCUPO in the off-policy setting. We propose a novel backward feature regression subroutine that reuses trajectories collected by past policies to estimate the occupancy measure of the current policy. Under suitable technical assumptions on the policy class (satisfied, e.g., by log-linear policies with sufficiently expressive features), we prove that the resulting algorithm achieves an $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity, up to a controllable projection error. We further extend our framework to linear MDPs and show that the resulting off-policy algorithm retains the same sample complexity. In these settings, the dependence on $\epsilon$ matches that for standard RL with linear function approximation. Moreover, our algorithms do not rely on the integral oracle required by prior work.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a model-based optimistic concave utility policy optimization (OCUPO) framework for reinforcement learning in bilinear MDPs. It leverages low-dimensional feature expectations to estimate occupancy measures efficiently, with both on-policy and off-policy variants.
data_sources: Not explicitly mentioned, but applicable to any financial data that can be modeled as episodic MDPs (e.g., sequential trading decisions, portfolio optimization).
alpha_potential: Potential applications in automated trading strategies where sequential decision-making under uncertainty is key. The framework's efficiency improvements could be valuable for high-frequency or algorithmic trading systems.

title: Maco-RL: Scaling Agent Capabilities with Mixed-Task Reinforcement Learning
summary: Mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) directly trains a unified policy across domains to continually expand agent capabilities without training separate specialists or requiring an extra distillation stage. Despite its appeal, scaling MixRL poses significant challenges in achieving stable and efficient mixed-task learning, effectively allocating rollout compute, and supporting continual domain expansion. To address these challenges, we propose Maco-RL, an approach that effectively scales MixRL. Specifically, Maco-RL employs a quota-based scheduler for asynchronous rollouts across multiple task domains, thereby stabilizing training by balancing gradient contributions and mitigating off-policy effects. Along an orthogonal axis, Maco-RL further introduces Tri-Buffer Sampling (TBS) to allocate compute among samples with varying levels of mastery, promoting sustained frontier exploration while preserving acquired capabilities. Experiments on five benchmarks show Maco-RL raises Qwen3.5-27B's overall score from 43.6 to 54.2 and then to 60.1 with continual expansion, reaching the frontier held by Qwen3.8-27B, which is further pushed outward by +5.7. Maco-RL also outperforms single-task RL with less compute for policy updates. These results support MixRL as a practical and compute-efficient post-training approach with substantial potential to strengthen general agent capabilities.
core_methodology: Mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) with quota-based scheduling and Tri-Buffer Sampling (TBS) to stabilize training and allocate compute efficiently across multiple task domains.

title: BRIAR: Martingale Belief Smoothing on Bifurcation-Guided Reasoning Trees
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has rapidly advanced long-chain reasoning, yet standard policy optimizers distribute rollout compute and gradient credit blindly across a trajectory. On hard problems, an early misstep derails the remaining trace, whereas on solvable problems, the policy keeps generating redundant verification long after the answer is already determined. We trace both pathologies to a single structural fact: under an on-policy verifier, the true prefix pass probability $V^\pi(u)$ along a reasoning trace forms a $[0,1]$-bounded Doob martingale whose learnable credit variance is strictly conserved and bounded above by $V^\pi(u)(1-V^\pi(u))$, vanishing at both the derailed ($V^\pi\to 0$) and absorbed ($V^\pi\to 1$) boundaries. We introduce BRIAR (Bifurcation-guided Rollout and Inference on Adaptive Reasoning trees), a tree-structured RLVR framework built directly around this martingale geometry. First, BRIAR expands discourse-aligned reasoning trees along an upper-confidence outcome-bifurcation frontier, steering rollouts away from absorbed rumination and toward unresolved decision points. Second, it models latent node values with boundary-scaled heteroscedastic edge variances and computes exact global posteriors in linear $\mathcal{O}(|V|)$ time via two-pass Rauch--Tung--Striebel (RTS) tree belief smoothing, eliminating $\mathcal{O}(m^3)$ matrix inversions while gating out spurious boundary noise. Third, BRIAR detects minimal absorbed frontier nodes and applies zero-sum log-length centered suffix advantages strictly post-absorption, leaving pre-absorption derivations provably invariant.
core_methodology: BRIAR is a tree-structured RLVR framework that utilizes martingale geometry and bifurcation-guided reasoning to optimize reinforcement learning. It focuses on efficiently directing computational resources to unresolved decision points in reasoning trees, preventing redundant computations and improving performance on hard problems.

title: Gradient TD($\lambda$) for Non-Linear Function Approximation
summary: Temporal difference (TD) learning is central to reinforcement learning. Many methods use semi-gradient TD, which may diverge, or develop algorithms with mean-squared Bellman or TD-error objectives that are difficult to analyze. Gradient TD algorithms overcome these challenges by using projection of the value function and present convergent off-policy algorithms. However, the algorithm for $\lambda$-return was limited to linear function approximation. Here, we extend the same to non-linear function approximation, which is desirable since many strong modern function approximators are complex and non-linear. Recent works have derived similar algorithms with a generalized projected Bellman error objective. Alternatively, we continue working with the projected Bellman error.
core_methodology: Gradient TD(λ) for non-linear function approximation in reinforcement learning, focusing on convergent off-policy algorithms with projected Bellman error

title: Provably Efficient Offline Discounted Reinforcement Learning under Recursive Entropic Risk
summary: We study risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in finite discounted infinite-horizon Markov Decision Processes with recursive entropic risk measures (ERM), parameterized by $\beta\neq 0$. We consider both risk-averse ($\beta>0$) and risk-seeking ($\beta<0$) settings. We consider the offline RL setting, where the agent is provided with a fixed dataset and wishes to learn a near-optimal policy using this dataset. We introduce a model-based algorithm, called ERM Value Iteration Lower Confidence Bound (ERM-VI-LCB) and derive a PAC-type bound on its sample complexity. We also establish a corresponding lower bound, demonstrating that exponential dependence on $|\beta|/(1-\gamma)$ asserted by the upper bound is unavoidable in the worst case. The presented bounds provide the first rigorous sample complexity guarantees for offline RL under recursive ERM across both risk-averse and risk-seeking regimes.
core_methodology: Model-based offline reinforcement learning with recursive entropic risk measures (ERM), applicable to both risk-averse and risk-seeking settings. The algorithm, ERM-VI-LCB, provides PAC-type sample complexity guarantees.
data_sources: Fixed dataset provided for offline learning, which could theoretically include historical market data or simulated trading environments.
alpha_potential: The approach could potentially be adapted for developing risk-sensitive trading strategies, particularly in scenarios where risk-adjusted returns are prioritized, such as portfolio optimization or algorithmic trading under uncertainty.

title: Improved Sample Complexity of Robust Reinforcement Learning with KL Uncertainty Sets
summary: In this paper, we study distributionally robust reinforcement learning with Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence-defined uncertainty sets. The goal is to find a policy that maximizes the robust value function, defined as the worst-case value over all transition kernels in the uncertainty set. Assuming access to a generative model, we aim to understand the sample complexity of finding an $\epsilon$-optimal robust policy. The best-known sample complexity results in the literature show a non-trivial gap of $\mathcal{O}\{\max\{p_\wedge^{-1}(1-\gamma)^{-1},(1-\gamma)^{-2}\}\}$ between the upper and lower bounds, where $p_\wedge$ denotes the minimum positive transition probability of the nominal transition kernel, and $\gamma$ is the discount factor. More importantly, existing results on the lower bound only cover a limited range of the uncertainty level. In this paper, we develop tighter and complete upper and lower bounds for robust RL with KL-defined uncertainty sets. Our upper bound is the tightest among all existing studies, and it improves upon the best-known bound by at least the order of $\mathcal{O}(\min\{p_\wedge^{-1},(1-\gamma)^{-1}\})$ for uncertainty level $\delta\in(0,1)$. Furthermore, our lower bound holds for any uncertainty level. Our upper and lower bounds (nearly) match in various regimes, providing improved results for this problem.
core_methodology: Distributionally robust reinforcement learning with Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence-defined uncertainty sets to optimize policies under worst-case transition kernels.
data_sources: Theoretical study assuming access to a generative model, not specific to financial data but applicable to simulated market environments.
alpha_potential: Potential for creating robust trading strategies that can perform well under various market conditions by considering worst-case scenarios, particularly useful for risk management in algorithmic trading.

title: RHOPE: LLM-Augmented Adaptive Experimental Design with Complex Contextual Information
summary: Experimental design allocates limited measurement effort across candidate treatments to learn their expected outcomes. Adaptive designs refine allocations as evidence accumulates, improving estimation and treatment selection. Contextual information can inform these decisions, but exploiting unstructured or high-dimensional context remains challenging. We use large language models (LLMs) to transform complex context into proxy outcomes and propose Residual Horizon Optimization for Prediction-Powered Experimentation (RHOPE), a principled Bayesian adaptive experimentation framework that combines true outcomes with LLM-generated proxy outcomes and formulates finite-batch design as a posterior Markov decision process (MDP). Our methodology uses proxy outcomes in two ways: sample augmentation improves estimation precision, while observing proxies before each allocation decision provides advance information. Synthetic experiments and semi-synthetic experiments using Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) data suggest that estimation precision drives most gains, with smaller advance-information gains, and highlight the importance of proxy informativeness and moment-estimation accuracy.
core_methodology: The paper presents RHOPE, a Bayesian adaptive experimentation framework that leverages LLM-generated proxy outcomes and formulates the experimental design as a posterior Markov decision process (MDP). It uses proxy outcomes for sample augmentation and pre-allocation decision-making.
data_sources: The paper uses synthetic experiments and semi-synthetic experiments with Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) data. While not financial, the methodology could be adapted to market data.
alpha_potential: The methodology could potentially be adapted to improve portfolio optimization or asset selection by using LLM-generated proxies to enhance estimation precision and decision-making in dynamic market conditions.

title: QPAT: A Universal Quantum Machine Learning Framework for Quantum-Assisted Training and Classical Inference
summary: Deep learning models often struggle with sharp local optima and overfitting in limited-data regimes, and exhibit limited capacity for capturing high-order, complex probability distributions. Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models, by operating in exponentially large Hilbert spaces, can efficiently represent such distributions and provide favorable inductive biases for learning, offering a promising pathway to overcome these limitations. However, their practical deployment in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era is severely hindered by gradient coupling, barren plateaus, data-loading bottlenecks, and high inference latency. To bridge classical AI and QML, we propose QPAT (QCBM-Prior-Assisted Training), a universal framework that employs a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) as a learnable generative prior to provide a task-aligned structured inductive bias during classical model training. The framework can be seamlessly integrated into any classical backbone, including LSTMs, CNNs, and Transformers. We introduce a decoupled fitness-based scoring mechanism and a stochastic "Drop-Prior" mechanism to implicitly distill quantum structural knowledge into the classical weights during training. Evaluated extensively on six benchmarks spanning time-series forecasting, computer vision, and natural language processing, our framework consistently outperforms purely classical backbones in both predictive performance and stability across random seeds; ablation studies further show that these gains are not reproduced by unstructured random priors or a classically learned generative prior. Remarkably, our approach enables completely classical inference, bypassing quantum latency while preserving quantum-enhanced accuracy, paving a highly practical path for QML deployment.
core_methodology: The paper proposes QPAT, a Quantum Machine Learning (QML) framework that uses a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) as a learnable generative prior to enhance classical model training. The framework includes a decoupled fitness-based scoring mechanism and a stochastic "Drop-Prior" mechanism to distill quantum structural knowledge into classical weights during training, enabling classical inference with quantum-enhanced accuracy.

However, the direct applicability to financial markets requires further empirical validation.

title: Accelerated Proximal Gradient Methods for Multiobjective Optimization over Probability Measures via Hilbert-Space Lifting
summary: Many sampling and inference tasks require a single distribution that balances several targets. We formulate this task as multiobjective optimization of Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergences over probability measures, in the Pareto sense. The particle method MWGraD (Nguyen et al., 2025) uses explicit Wasserstein gradient steps, and its accelerated version A-MWGraD (Nguyen et al., 2026) lacks discrete-time guarantees. We propose the multiobjective Wasserstein proximal gradient (MWPG), which uses implicit Wasserstein gradient steps, and its accelerated version, multiobjective Wasserstein accelerated proximal gradient (MWAPG), with rigorous discrete-time guarantees. Our key idea is a Hilbert-space lifting: each measure is represented as the pushforward of a fixed base measure by a map in a Hilbert space. The problem then becomes a constrained multiobjective composite problem over transport maps, to which accelerated proximal gradient methods apply. For convex and smooth potentials, we show that MWAPG decreases a Pareto merit function at the rate $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$; for $m$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth potentials, the rate is $\mathcal{O}\big((1-\sqrt{m/L})^k\big)$. We also give closed-form Gaussian updates and particle implementations based on input-convex neural networks, which require no score estimation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world dataset show that MWAPG needs far fewer iterations than MWPG and matches or outperforms A-MWGraD in Bayesian multi-task learning.
core_methodology: The paper presents the multiobjective Wasserstein proximal gradient (MWPG) and its accelerated version (MWAPG) for multiobjective optimization over probability measures using Hilbert-space lifting. It focuses on balancing several targets through KL divergences and uses implicit Wasserstein gradient steps with rigorous discrete-time guarantees.

title: LatENSO v1.0: a learned latent state of the tropical Pacific for seasonal ENSO operators and forecasting
summary: Here we present LatENSO v1.0, a machine-learning forecast system for the El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) built around a learned, 32-dimensional state of the tropical Pacific. A Swin-transformer autoencoder compresses thirteen monthly-averaged ocean and atmosphere fields into 32 numbers, trained to reconstruct the fields, with no forecast target. The 32 numbers rebuild the fields as well as O(100) empirical orthogonal functions. Two seasonal operators use this state. The first is the extended nonlinear recharge oscillator (XRO) with two directions of the learned state among its variables; we call it XRO-lat. The second is a Floquet modal operator (FMO) of three damped oscillators, which forecasts a correction added to a least-squares base forecast made from four observed predictors. We evaluate both against the recharge oscillator, XRO and a deep echo-state network (DESN), all refitted on identical data, cross-validation folds and verification windows (1981-2024). Over lead times of 1-18 months, XRO-lat reaches an anomaly correlation coefficient (ACC) of 0.673, the highest of all tropical-Pacific-only (in-domain) systems and statistically indistinguishable from XRO and DESN with their eight remote-basin indices (0.685 and 0.667). From lead 15 to lead 24 it is the most skillful of all systems. Over leads 1-18, the FMO forecast (0.619) is statistically indistinguishable from every in-domain reference model (0.631-0.654). What the FMO adds to its base forecast, 0.054 in ACC, is carried by its Floquet propagation, whose generator consistently holds a prominent quasi-biennial oscillator. At leads 3-9 the FMO trails XRO, DESN and the in-domain XRO, a deficit partly attributable to its base. LatENSO combines competitive skill with trustworthiness: a compact state whose physical content can be inspected, and fully open access to code, weights and data.
core_methodology: The paper presents a machine-learning forecast system for the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) using a Swin-transformer autoencoder to compress and reconstruct oceanic and atmospheric data. It also introduces two seasonal operators: an extended nonlinear recharge oscillator (XRO-lat) and a Floquet modal operator (FMO) for forecasting corrections.
data_sources: Thirteen monthly-averaged ocean and atmosphere fields from the tropical Pacific region, covering the period from 1981 to 2024.
alpha_potential: The system's ability to forecast ENSO events with competitive skill could be leveraged in commodity markets, particularly in trading agricultural commodities, energy futures, and other assets sensitive to climate conditions influenced by ENSO. The quasi-biennial oscillator identified in the Floquet propagation could provide a periodic signal for timing strategies.

title: SACA: Selective Attention-Based Clustering Algorithm
summary: Clustering algorithms are fundamental tools across many fields, with density-based methods offering particular advantages in identifying arbitrarily shaped clusters and handling noise. However, their effectiveness is often limited by the requirement of critical parameter tuning by users, which typically requires significant domain expertise. This paper introduces a novel density-based clustering algorithm loosely inspired by the concept of selective attention, designed to minimize reliance on parameter tuning for most applications. The proposed method computes an adaptive threshold to exclude sparsely distributed points and outliers, constructs an initial cluster framework, and subsequently reintegrates the filtered points to refine the final results. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate the robustness, accuracy, and ease of use of the proposed approach, establishing it as a powerful alternative to conventional density-based clustering techniques.
core_methodology: A novel density-based clustering algorithm inspired by selective attention, designed to minimize parameter tuning. The method computes an adaptive threshold to exclude outliers, constructs initial clusters, and reintegrates filtered points for final refinement.
data_sources: Benchmark datasets (not specified for financial applications, but methodology could be applied to market data).
alpha_potential: Potential for identifying non-linear patterns in financial time series or asset clusters without extensive parameter tuning, which could be valuable for portfolio construction or anomaly detection.

title: ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$: Temporal Distribution Shift Generalization for Industry-Scale Recommender Systems
summary: Temporal distribution shift (TDS) degrades the generalization of recommender systems: models trained on past interactions face systematically different user behavior in future time windows. While incremental training on recent data is widely used in industrial production, it can over-adapt to transient patterns and exacerbate instability. Existing approaches such as invariant learning and self-supervised learning offer partial solutions but often suffer from unstable temporal generalization, representation collapse, or inefficient data utilization. To address these limitations, we propose ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$, a probabilistic framework for temporally robust recommendation. First, we identify key shifting factors in real-world production data and design a simple yet effective data augmentation strategy that simulates realistic time-varying factors and expands the training support. Second, we derive a self-supervised variational objective, ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$, to harness the benefits of this extended distribution while preventing representation collapse. Extensive experiments on both a public benchmark and a large-scale industrial dataset demonstrate that ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$ consistently improves next-period ranking performance over strong baselines. It achieves a 2.33\% uplift in GMV per user in online experiments and has been successfully deployed in production. Code is available at https://github.com/FuCongResearchSquad/ELBO4TDS
core_methodology: The paper introduces ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$, a probabilistic framework combining data augmentation and self-supervised variational objectives to improve temporal generalization in recommender systems. The methodology focuses on handling temporal distribution shifts by simulating realistic time-varying factors and preventing representation collapse.
data_sources: The paper uses both a public benchmark dataset and a large-scale industrial dataset from recommender systems, which includes user interaction data over time.
alpha_potential: The framework's ability to adapt to temporal shifts could be valuable for quantitative trading strategies that rely on time-series data, such as momentum or mean-reversion strategies, where market behavior changes over time. The data augmentation and variational approach might help in modeling evolving market regimes or investor behavior.

title: Localized Dynamics-Aware Domain Adaptation for Off-Dynamics Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Off-dynamics offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn a policy for a target domain using limited target data and abundant source data collected under different transition dynamics. Existing methods typically address dynamics mismatch either globally over the state space or via pointwise data filtering; these approaches can miss localized cross-domain similarities or incur high computational cost. We propose Localized Dynamics-Aware Domain Adaptation (LoDADA), which exploits localized dynamics mismatch to better reuse source data. LoDADA clusters transitions from source and target datasets and estimates cluster-level dynamics discrepancy via domain discrimination. Source transitions from clusters with small discrepancy are more likely to be retained compared with those from clusters with large discrepancy. This yields a fine-grained and scalable data selection strategy that avoids overly coarse global assumptions and expensive per-sample filtering. We provide theoretical insights and extensive experiments across environments with diverse global and local dynamics shifts. Results show that LoDADA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art off-dynamics offline RL methods by better leveraging localized distribution mismatch.
core_methodology: Localized Dynamics-Aware Domain Adaptation (LoDADA) for Off-Dynamics Offline Reinforcement Learning, which clusters transitions from source and target datasets and estimates cluster-level dynamics discrepancy via domain discrimination.
data_sources: Source and target datasets collected under different transition dynamics, potentially including simulated or historical market data.
alpha_potential: The methodology could be adapted to optimize trading strategies by better leveraging localized similarities across different market regimes or asset classes, potentially improving robustness to regime shifts.

title: Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Memory-Efficient Latent Chain-of-Thought with Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization
summary: Standard Transformers have a fixed computational depth, limiting their ability to generalize to tasks that require variable-depth reasoning. The usual remedy, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), spends tokens to reason, inflating the key--value cache, so memory becomes the limiting cost when reasoning is served over large query batches. We study a depth-recurrent Transformer that decouples computational depth from parameter count by iterating a shared-weight block, so that adding reasoning steps leaves peak inference memory unchanged and grows latency only linearly, with no token generation. Three ingredients support the recurrence over 20+ thinking steps: a silent thinking objective that supervises only the final output, LayerScale initialization, and an identity-biased gate that opens a gradient highway across steps. We characterize it on three compositional domains with decreasing structural bias: graph reachability (adjacency masking), nested boolean logic (relative positioning), and unstructured relational text (no structural positional cue). We find a \emph{computational frontier}: accuracy climbs once the thinking-step count meets the task's complexity, reaching near-perfect performance on the two structured tasks and a lower plateau on unstructured text. How it climbs depends on the structural bias---abruptly from chance on the graph task, gradually on the other two. Depth recurrence extrapolates beyond the training range: it succeeds on the graph task where fixed-depth models barely extrapolate, and on the two sequence tasks comes within two points of fixed-depth Transformers that use $4$--$6.4\times$ more parameters. On the graph task, whose adjacency mask makes propagation depth verifiable, intermediate per-step supervision---a standard recipe for deep iterative models---consistently \emph{harms} this extrapolation at widths $d \geq 256$. We release the code for reproducibility.
core_methodology: Depth-recurrent Transformer with shared-weight blocks for variable-depth reasoning without memory inflation
data_sources: Three compositional domains: graph reachability, nested boolean logic, unstructured relational text (no financial market data)
alpha_potential: Potential for complex reasoning in market microstructure analysis or factor combination strategies where variable-depth processing is beneficial

title: Recurrent In-Context Learning for Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Tabular foundation models predict unlabelled rows from labelled rows in a single forward pass via in-context learning (ICL). Like language models, these architectures have scaled by stacking transformer blocks, each with its own parameters. However, this approach couples compute with model size: increasing computation requires increasing the parameter count. In this work, we investigate whether tabular ICL requires distinct parameters at every block, or simply sufficient depth. We introduce Tab-Loop, a looped tabular foundation model built on the TabICLv2 architecture. Instead of stacking unique blocks, Tab-Loop takes a small set of blocks with shared parameters and applies them repeatedly in a loop during its ICL stage. We evaluate this design against standard architectures under equal training and inference compute budgets. Our experiments show that depth, rather than unique parameters, drives performance. Across classification and regression tasks on held-out synthetic tables, the TabArena and TALENT benchmarks, Tab-Loop matches the accuracy of a standard model with three times as many ICL blocks while using roughly 60% fewer parameters. Conversely, a non-looped baseline of the same size as Tab-Loop underperforms it, even when trained on 32% more tables. This pattern holds consistently whether we vary the number of distinct blocks from one to twelve or the effective depth. Furthermore, running additional loops at inference improves predictive accuracy without retraining. Training the model with deeper loops extends the range over which these extra inference steps remain beneficial, eventually matching the released TabICLv2 on TabArena at 2.7 times the ICL compute. These results show that tabular foundation models can scale their compute independently of parameter count, pointing to test-time compute scaling as a practical path toward efficient tabular models.
core_methodology: The paper introduces Tab-Loop, a looped tabular foundation model that utilizes shared parameters across blocks and applies them repeatedly during in-context learning (ICL). This approach decouples compute from model size, allowing for efficient scaling of compute independently of parameter count.
data_sources: The paper evaluates performance on held-out synthetic tables, the TabArena benchmark, and the TALENT benchmark. While not financial data, the methodology could be adapted for financial datasets such as stock prices, trading volumes, or other structured financial data.
alpha_potential: The methodology's ability to scale compute independently of parameter count could be valuable in developing efficient trading models that require real-time inference. The in-context learning approach might also be useful for generating trading signals from structured data, though the paper does not directly address financial applications.

title: Conditional Flow Models Convert Epistemic Uncertainty into Apparent Aleatoric Variance
summary: Conditional Flow Models (CFMs) are increasingly being used in place of deterministic predictors across machine learning, including for tasks that were classically formulated as regression. Given their success in such tasks, we ask the question: what useful information do the conditional distributions produced by CFMs carry beyond what a point predictor would provide? We identify a systematic phenomenon: in many natural regimes, CFM samples routinely have larger variance than the true conditional distribution, even in nearly deterministic regression problems. This effect is most pronounced where the model has not resolved the dependence on the conditioning variable, and thus the additional variance can be viewed as converting \emph{epistemic uncertainty} in fitting the ground truth conditional distribution into apparent \emph{aleatoric variance} in the generated samples. Through controlled synthetic and real-data experiments, and comparisons with explicit smoothing estimators, we show that the induced variance tracks model underfitting of complex or hard-to-fit targets, and decreases with additional training or data. We uncover surprising structure in this excess conditional variance that seems unique to CFMs and absent in the other standard probabilistic models that we test. We provide a theoretical account of the phenomenon in a simplified setting and demonstrate a consequent practical use-case of conditional flow-matching: designing high-coverage predictive sets that cover the ground-truth regression target.
core_methodology: Conditional Flow Models (CFMs) are used to generate conditional distributions that convert epistemic uncertainty into apparent aleatoric variance, providing more nuanced probabilistic outputs than deterministic predictors.
data_sources: The paper mentions synthetic and real-data experiments, though specific financial datasets are not detailed.
alpha_potential: CFMs could enhance predictive uncertainty modeling in trading strategies, particularly in scenarios where traditional point predictors fail to capture complex dependencies or underfitting issues. This could improve risk assessment and predictive set coverage in algorithmic trading.

title: When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents
summary: Human annotations on documents (such as arrows, carets, strikethroughs, and insertions) express corrective intent yet existing OCR and document understanding systems treat these marks as visual noise rather than semantic edit operations. We introduce intent-aware OCR, the task of generating corrected transcriptions by jointly reasoning over original document content and visual intent cues (handwritten or digital) that convey edit intent. To support this setting, we present DocIntent, a multimodal dataset of 1,600 financial documents with over 5,700 annotated visual intent cues, each paired with layout-aware, intent-resolved OCR targets. We further introduce IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark designed to evaluate model robustness under diverse real-world annotation conditions. Leveraging DocIntent, we fine-tune DocIntentOCR, a suite of 3B and 7B parameter vision-language models, under direct intent supervision on corrected transcriptions. On IntentBench, the fine-tuned 3B and 7B models achieve F1-scores of 0.81 and 0.83, respectively, substantially outperforming commercial closed-source (e.g., GPT-4.1 (0.626)), and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B (0.50)) demonstrating that intent-aware supervision enables compact domain-specific models to outperform substantially larger general-purpose systems on this task. This work establishes intent-aware OCR as a novel human-in-the-loop document understanding task and provides foundational resources (dataset, benchmark, models) to advance research in interactive document processing.
core_methodology: The paper introduces intent-aware OCR, which leverages vision-language models (VLMs) to interpret human annotations (e.g., arrows, carets) as semantic edit operations, generating corrected transcriptions of financial documents.
data_sources: DocIntent dataset comprising 1,600 financial documents with 5,700 annotated visual intent cues, paired with layout-aware, intent-resolved OCR targets.
alpha_potential: Potential to improve data accuracy in financial document processing, which could enhance quantitative models relying on cleaned and corrected financial data. However, direct trading alpha is not explicitly demonstrated.

title: Neur2BiLO: Neural Bilevel Optimization
summary: Bilevel optimization deals with nested problems in which a leader takes the first decision to minimize their objective function while accounting for a follower's best-response reaction. Constrained bilevel problems with integer variables are particularly notorious for their hardness. While exact solvers have been proposed for mixed-integer linear bilevel optimization, they tend to scale poorly with problem size and are hard to generalize to the non-linear case. On the other hand, problem-specific algorithms (exact and heuristic) are limited in scope. Under a data-driven setting in which similar instances of a bilevel problem are solved routinely, our proposed framework, Neur2BiLO, embeds a neural network approximation of the leader's or follower's value function, trained via supervised regression, into an easy-to-solve mixed-integer program. Neur2BiLO serves as a heuristic that produces high-quality solutions extremely fast for four applications with linear and non-linear objectives and pure and mixed-integer variables.
core_methodology: Neural network approximation of value functions in bilevel optimization problems, embedded into mixed-integer programming.
data_sources: Data-driven setting with similar instances of bilevel problems solved routinely.
alpha_potential: Potential for optimizing decision-making in hierarchical financial systems, such as portfolio optimization with constraints or strategic trading decisions.

title: A Unifying Framework for Robust and Efficient Inference with Unstructured Data
summary: AI can cheaply extract structured variables from unstructured data, with alternative implementation choices potentially yielding different measures of the same concept. This creates a credibility challenge, effectively moving specification search upstream. We confront this challenge with MAR-S (Missing At Random Structured Data), a framework which adapts semiparametric missing data theory to deliver valid, efficient, robust inference with AI predictions. MAR-S anchors measurement in a transparent validation sample design, while AI scales measurement. We provide general recipes for MAR-S estimation and extend the framework to aggregated and transformed AI predictions, a common setting not addressed by existing frameworks.
core_methodology: MAR-S (Missing At Random Structured Data) framework, adapting semiparametric missing data theory for robust and efficient inference with AI predictions
data_sources: Unstructured data processed by AI to extract structured variables, with a focus on transparent validation sample design
alpha_potential: Potential to improve signal extraction from unstructured data (e.g., news, social media, earnings calls) with robust statistical guarantees, applicable to sentiment analysis or alternative data strategies

title: Stability Regularized Cross-Validation
summary: We study hyperparameter selection via cross-validation, motivated by settings in which the selected $k$-fold cross-validation error underestimates the selected model's test error. We propose a nested $k$-fold cross-validation scheme that minimizes a weighted sum of the standard cross-validation error and empirical hypothesis stability, with the stability weight selected by an outer cross-validation loop. We derive a generalization bound that controls test error using the cross-validation error and empirical hypothesis stability, together with correction terms common to every candidate. In a stylized ridge regression setting, we then show that whether the stability weight improves expected test-set performance depends on the signal-to-noise ratio, with the greatest improvement when the signal-to-noise ratio is small. On $13$ real-world regression datasets, the procedure reduces the average out-of-sample MSE relative to $k$-fold cross-validation by $5.6\%$ for sparse regression and by $6.8\%$ for CART. A side benefit of an outer cross-validation loop is that the selected error estimates are better calibrated than those from ordinary $k$-fold cross-validation: the error estimate moves from 12.3\% below the selected test-set MSE to 5.8\% above it for sparse regression and from 10.3\% below to 0.2\% above it for CART.
core_methodology: Nested k-fold cross-validation scheme that incorporates empirical hypothesis stability, optimized via an outer cross-validation loop. Applied to ridge regression, sparse regression, and CART models.
data_sources: 13 real-world regression datasets (unspecified domain, but methodology is domain-agnostic).
alpha_potential: Potential to improve model selection for trading strategies by reducing out-of-sample MSE, particularly in low signal-to-noise ratio environments common in financial markets. Better calibration of error estimates could lead to more reliable strategy backtesting.
