title: BayesFlow 2: Multi-Backend Amortized Bayesian Inference in Python
summary: Modern Bayesian inference involves a mixture of computational methods for estimating, validating, and drawing conclusions from probabilistic models as part of principled workflows. An overarching motif of many Bayesian methods is that they are relatively slow, which often becomes prohibitive when fitting complex models to large data sets. Amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) offers a path to solving the computational challenges of Bayes. ABI trains neural networks on model simulations, rewarding users with rapid inference of any model-implied quantity, such as point estimates, likelihoods, or full posterior distributions. In this work, we present the Python library BayesFlow, Version 2, for general-purpose ABI. Along with direct posterior, likelihood, and ratio estimation, the software includes support for multiple popular deep learning backends, a rich collection of generative networks for sampling and density estimation, complete customization and high-level interfaces, as well as new capabilities for hyperparameter optimization, design optimization, and multilevel modeling. Using a case study on dynamical system parameter estimation, combined with comparisons to similar software, we show that our streamlined, user-friendly workflow has strong potential to support broad adoption.
core_methodology: Amortized Bayesian Inference (ABI) using neural networks trained on model simulations, enabling rapid estimation of posterior distributions, likelihoods, and other model-implied quantities.
data_sources: Model simulations, potentially applicable to synthetic or empirical financial time series data.
alpha_potential: Potential to improve Bayesian inference in high-frequency trading and portfolio optimization by enabling faster and more scalable posterior estimation, which could lead to more efficient parameter estimation and risk assessment.

title: Effect-Driven Skill Abstractions for Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: We seek to learn discrete skill abstractions to facilitate long-horizon, goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning (RL) tasks. Recent approaches have shown success by quantizing actions via clustering or reconstruction. However, these objectives lead to skills that are not directly related to what the current state affords or what the goal requires. Instead, we argue that goal-directed skills should be driven by \emph{how they affect the state} of the agent. To realize this, we introduce a novel quantization method for action chunks that optimizes next-state predictions conditioned on the current state and action. This objective encourages skills to be distinguished by the future states they lead to, resulting in a vocabulary that spans diverse outcomes reachable from a given state. Our framework can easily be paired with common offline RL methods by replacing their continuous actor head with a discrete one that selects among the learned skills. We can execute these skills in the environment by converting them back to continuous actions using a trained low-level controller. Experiments on benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks largely show substantial and consistent improvements over both the continuous-actor baselines and reconstruction-based discretizations. Our project page can be found at: https://burcukilic.github.io/projects/effect-driven-skill-abstractions/.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a novel quantization method for action chunks in reinforcement learning that focuses on next-state predictions rather than action clustering or reconstruction. This method aims to create discrete skills based on their effect on the agent's state, which can be integrated into offline RL frameworks.
data_sources: The paper does not specify financial data sources but rather focuses on benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks, which could be analogously applied to financial market data.
alpha_potential: The methodology could potentially be adapted for developing trading strategies by creating discrete skill sets (e.g., buy, hold, sell) based on their predicted market impact, which could lead to more effective decision-making in automated trading systems.

title: Differentially Private Policy Optimization in Linear MDPs with Adversarial Rewards
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) in personalized services often relies on sensitive interaction data. Motivated by the need to protect these data, we study differentially private (DP) policy optimization in episodic linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with unknown transitions and adaptive adversarial linear rewards under full-information feedback. This setting poses two key challenges: past trajectories are repeatedly reused for policy evaluation, and reward choices may depend on previously released private statistics. The proposed algorithm combines batched proximal policy optimization (PPO) updates with optimistic policy evaluation, using private regression statistics and reward estimates to protect both trajectories and reward functions under joint differential privacy (JDP). With all other parameters fixed, our high-probability regret bound retains the same leading $\widetilde{O}\left(K^{3/4}\right)$ dependence on the number of episodes $K$ as the corresponding non-private bound for batched optimistic PPO. The additional privacy terms scale as $\widetilde{O} \left(K^{5/8}\right)$ and $\widetilde{O} \left(K^{1/2}\right)$. Thus, privacy incurs only lower-order additive costs in $K$, even under adaptive adversarial rewards.
core_methodology: The paper presents a differentially private (DP) policy optimization algorithm for linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with adversarial rewards, combining batched proximal policy optimization (PPO) updates with optimistic policy evaluation. It uses private regression statistics and reward estimates to protect both trajectories and reward functions under joint differential privacy (JDP).
data_sources: The data sources involve episodic interaction data from personalized services, which in a financial context could be analogous to sensitive trading or portfolio management data.
alpha_potential: The method could potentially be adapted to protect sensitive trading strategies or portfolio optimization processes from adversarial attacks or data leaks, thereby preserving alpha in competitive environments. The adversarial reward setting is particularly relevant for modeling market reactions to trading actions.
title_cn: 线性马尔可夫决策过程中具有对抗性奖励的差分隐私策略优化

title: Put the World Back: Timestamps Matter in Time Series Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to time series reasoning. However, current evaluations often give models events in chronological order and already matched to the time series. This makes it unclear whether models use timestamps to connect events with observations or simply take shortcuts. To expose this ambiguity, we reformulate time series reasoning from a world-to-series projection perspective, viewing timestamps as explicit indices that connect numerical observations and external events to shared world states. We identify three structures that timestamps can make explicit: temporal causal structure, time semantics, and event-series alignment. Building on this perspective, we develop a diagnostic protocol that distinguishes timestamp-grounded reasoning from correlational shortcuts, a distinction that accuracy-based benchmarks cannot make. Controlled interventions on 310 questions from two tasks show that high accuracy can persist when timestamps are replaced by relative offsets or removed, while breaking event-series alignment induces systematic failures. When context is pre-aligned, models barely need timestamps. When order is missing, they use dates to recall world knowledge. Without dates, they rely on correlational shortcuts and rarely notice incorrect timestamps. These findings show that high accuracy on pre-aligned, ordered inputs does not establish that a model uses timestamps to synchronize observations with the world. We release our code, model outputs, and trajectory labels at https://github.com/tingrui-huang/timestamps-matter.
core_methodology: Examines timestamp awareness in LLMs for time series reasoning, proposing a diagnostic protocol to assess whether models use timestamps for synchronization or rely on shortcuts.
data_sources: Not specified, likely synthetic or general time series datasets.
alpha_potential: Limited direct alpha potential, but could inform better time-aware AI models for financial time series analysis.

title: Adversarial Bandit Convex Optimization with $d^{3/2}\sqrt{n}$ Regret
summary: We study adversarial bandit convex optimization, where in each of $n$ rounds a learner chooses a point $A_t$ in a convex body $\mathcal{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ and observes only a noisy value of a convex loss $f_t:\mathcal{K}\to[0,1]$ at that point. The losses are chosen by an adversary, who may change them from round to round and adapt them to the learner's past actions. We improve the best known regret bound for this problem from $\widetilde O(d^{5/2}\sqrt n)$ (Lattimore, 2020, 2026) to $\widetilde O(d^{3/2}\sqrt n)$, which matches the rate conjectured by Bubeck et al. (2017). Together with the recent lower bound of $\Omega(d^{4/3}\sqrt n)$ due to Rajaraman and Han (2026), it determines the minimax regret up to a factor of $d^{1/6}$ and logarithmic factors. The algorithm is an online Newton step with Gaussian exploration. Unlike earlier methods of this kind, it uses unbiased estimates of the gradient and Hessian of the Gaussian smoothing of the loss, rather than of an optimistic surrogate.
core_methodology: Adversarial bandit convex optimization with online Newton step and Gaussian exploration
data_sources: Convex loss functions chosen by an adversary, potentially representing market conditions or portfolio performance metrics
alpha_potential: Potential for improved adaptive trading strategies in adversarial market conditions, optimizing portfolio choices under uncertainty

summary_cn: 该论文改进了对抗性强盗凸优化的遗憾界，提出了使用在线牛顿步和高斯探索的新算法。在金融交易中，这种方法可应用于动态投资组合优化，帮助交易系统在不确定性市场条件下更好地适应和调整决策。尽管理论性较强，但其算法框架为开发适应性交易策略提供了新思路。

title: Network of Theseus (like the ship)
summary: A standard assumption in deep learning is that the inductive bias introduced by a neural network architecture must persist from training through inference. The architecture you train with is the architecture you deploy. This assumption constrains the community from selecting architectures that may have desirable efficiency or design properties due to difficulties with optimization. We challenge this assumption with the Network of Theseus (NoT), a method for progressively converting a trained, or even untrained, guide network architecture part-by-part into an entirely different target network architecture while preserving the performance of the guide network. At each stage, components in the guide network architecture are incrementally replaced with the target architecture modules and aligned via representational similarity metrics. This procedure preserves most of the functionality of the guide network even under substantial architectural changes-for example, converting a convolutional network into a multilayer perceptron, or GPT-2 into a recurrent neural network. By decoupling optimization from deployment, NoT expands the space of viable inference-time architectures, opening opportunities for better accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs and enabling more directed exploration of the architectural design space.
core_methodology: Network of Theseus (NoT) is a method for progressively converting a trained or untrained guide network architecture into a different target network architecture while preserving performance. It uses representational similarity metrics to align components during the transition.
data_sources: No specific data sources mentioned in the abstract; the methodology is architecture-agnostic and could theoretically be applied to various types of financial data.
alpha_potential: Potential to optimize neural network architectures for financial models, leading to more efficient inference-time architectures. Could enable better tradeoffs between accuracy and computational efficiency in trading models.
title_cn: 忒修斯网络（类似忒修斯之船）
summary_cn: 忒修斯网络（NoT）通过在保持网络性能的同时逐步替换架构组件，实现了神经网络架构的灵活转换。这一方法可能用于优化量化交易中的模型计算效率，特别是在需要不同架构间迁移的场合，如从卷积网络转换到多层感知机，从而在保持预测能力的同时减少计算开销。

title: Fisher-R1: Training LLM Agents for Reliable Hypothesis Testing
summary: Reliable hypothesis testing is the foundation of many empirical scientific claims. Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to automate this process, as they can inspect datasets, generate code, and produce analyses end-to-end. However, we show that they frequently make subtle inferential errors that lead to incorrect conclusions despite correctly executed analyses. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this failure mode, as they rarely assess whether a reported p-value is statistically valid given the assumptions underlying the data. We address this gap by building P-Bench, a benchmark comprising 425 open-ended, realistic hypothesis-testing tasks spanning economics, biology, and medicine. Each task requires an agent to select a statistical method, compute a p-value, and draw a conclusion given only a scientific hypothesis and a dataset. We further introduce Fisher-R1, an open-weight LLM agent trained for rigorous hypothesis testing using synthetic tasks and reinforcement learning. On P-Bench, Fisher-R1-14B substantially improves over its backbone and outperforms strong proprietary and open-source baselines, including GPT-5.4 and DeepSeekV4-Pro, achieving a 21% average relative improvement in single-trial success over DeepSeek-V4-Pro, with gains up to 26% on the most challenging tasks. Our results demonstrate that current LLM agents lack reliable statistical reasoning for hypothesis testing and that reinforcement learning on tasks with verified statistical reward substantially improves reliability.
core_methodology: LLM agent trained for reliable statistical hypothesis testing using synthetic tasks and reinforcement learning
data_sources: Synthetic and realistic datasets spanning economics, biology, and medicine, but not explicitly financial markets
alpha_potential: Potential indirect benefits in improving econometric testing and statistical reasoning for quantitative trading models, though not directly applicable

title: LSTM-UT and Bounded Gated Memory for Looped Transformers
summary: Can the loop of a looped Transformer serve as a rollout, with one application of the shared block per step of a dynamical system? We started with two existing designs, one that carries only its residual stream and one, CoTFormer, that also caches every earlier state. On Rule 30, a chaotic cellular automaton, both lose the computation shortly after their trained depth. LSTM-UT, which adds an LSTM-style gated cell, does not, and it recalls earlier states better. Taking it apart shows that each ability has a simpler source. For rollouts it is decay: a fixed decay on the plain model's stream is sufficient. For recall it is an input-dependent gate: at the longest horizon a gated stream with no cell recalls as well as LSTM-UT, and no fixed decay helps. The two do not simply add, since a gated stream with a fixed decay does neither reliably. Storing every earlier state hurts extrapolation, where CoTFormer fits and rolls out further with its cache cut to the most recent repeat; in recall, the stored copy is looked up at the shortest horizon and not at the next. LSTM-UT, whose forget gate makes the decay itself input-dependent, is the only model in the leading group on both. The forget gate was added to the LSTM so that a state carried at weight one could be reset instead of accumulating; we find the same need over depth. In language modelling LSTM-UT is competitive with CoTFormer at lower training cost. Code is available at https://github.com/arskvnc22/lstm-ut
core_methodology: The paper introduces LSTM-UT, a gated memory mechanism for looped Transformers, to improve long-term memory and rollout capabilities in dynamical systems. It combines LSTM-style gating with Transformer architectures to enhance state recall and computational stability.
data_sources: The methodology is tested on Rule 30, a chaotic cellular automaton, and evaluated in language modeling tasks. No direct financial data sources are mentioned.
alpha_potential: The enhanced memory and rollout capabilities could be adapted for time-series prediction in financial markets, such as predicting price movements or volatility patterns, but the direct applicability is speculative without empirical testing on market data.
title_cn: LSTM-UT与有界门控内存：应用于循环Transformer的研究
summary_cn: 本研究提出了一种结合LSTM门控机制的循环Transformer（LSTM-UT），用于提升在动态系统中的长期记忆和计算稳定性。虽然当前测试基于混沌自动机，但其增强的时序处理能力可能适用于金融市场的时间序列预测，如价格或波动率建模。

title: Best Policy Tracking in Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning commonly exhibits non-monotonic performance dynamics in single-task settings. During learning, a sequence of policies is generated whose true performance is unknown and may oscillate significantly across iterations. Despite this well-known phenomenon, standard experimental practice typically reports either the final visited policy or the best among periodically evaluated ones, implicitly assuming that these selection criteria reliably approximate the best-performing policy visited throughout the entire sequence. In this work, we present an empirical study on the implications of non-monotonicity for policy selection in single-task policy-based reinforcement learning. We introduce post-hoc diagnostic metrics to characterize performance degradation and assess the accuracy and efficiency of different selection criteria. These metrics allow us to evaluate commonly used selection strategies across standard continuous-control benchmarks using a well-established on-policy actor-critic method. Our results show that, in this representative experimental setting, widely adopted selection practices can deviate considerably from the best policy encountered during learning, leading to underperforming estimates and suboptimal use of computational resources. As an alternative, we recommend a validation-based policy selection strategy constrained by computational cost, which provides a more consistent and accurate approximation of the best visited policy while improving selection efficiency. Overall, our findings highlight policy selection as an underexplored factor in the evaluation protocols of reinforcement learning and motivate further study on explicit and standardized validation-based selection procedures.
core_methodology: Empirical study on policy selection in single-task reinforcement learning, introducing diagnostic metrics and validation-based selection strategies.
data_sources: Standard continuous-control benchmarks (not financial data).
alpha_potential: Potential to improve reinforcement learning-based trading strategies by optimizing policy selection, but requires adaptation to financial contexts.
title_cn: 强化学习中的最优策略追踪
summary_cn: 该研究通过实证分析强化学习中的非单调性能动态，提出验证驱动的策略选择方法，对金融领域的强化学习交易策略优化具有借鉴意义，但需结合金融市场数据进行适配。

title: Improving fine-grained expressivity of graph neural networks
summary: This thesis investigates the expressive power of neural networks for structured data, focusing on graph neural networks and symmetry-aware architectures. We present four main contributions. First, we characterize the generic expressive power of geometric message-passing neural networks on sparse graphs and introduce EGenNet, an architecture achieving the corresponding guarantees. Second, we use representation theory to characterize linear layers equivariant to multiple permutations, including wreath-product symmetries. Third, we study permutation-invariant set representations that preserve containment, establish dimensional bounds and impossibility results, and introduce MASNet. Finally, we propose FSW-GNN, a message-passing architecture combining strong expressivity and bi-Lipschitz stability guarantees with strong empirical performance on long-range graph-learning tasks. Together, these results provide a broader understanding of how neural architectures can preserve the geometric, algebraic, order-theoretic, and metric structure of their inputs.
core_methodology: The paper focuses on enhancing the expressive power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) through novel architectures like EGenNet, MASNet, and FSW-GNN, which incorporate geometric, algebraic, and order-theoretic structures in graph data processing.
data_sources: The abstract does not specify particular data sources, but the methodologies imply potential application to structured financial data such as market graphs, transaction networks, or relational financial data.
alpha_potential: The improved expressivity and stability of GNNs could enhance the modeling of complex financial networks, potentially uncovering hidden patterns in market microstructure, asset correlations, or arbitrage opportunities.
title_cn: 提升图神经网络的细粒度表达能力
summary_cn: 该论文通过增强图神经网络（GNN）的表达能力，提出了EGenNet、MASNet和FSW-GNN等新型架构，结合几何、代数和序理论结构。这些方法在金融网络建模中可能发现市场微观结构或资产关联中的隐藏模式，为量化交易策略开发提供了理论基础。

title: A Fused Gaussian Process Bandit Framework for Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization
summary: Bayesian optimization (BO) is widely used to maximize expensive black-box functions when direct evaluation is costly. In many real-world applications, the high-fidelity objective can be approximated by a series of lower-fidelity models that provide partial but informative signals at substantially reduced cost. Multi-fidelity BO (MFBO) algorithms aim to strategically combine these information sources to achieve an optimal trade-off between accuracy and evaluation cost. However, existing MFBO methods often oversimplify the complex dependencies between fidelity levels or rely on heuristic acquisition functions that lack theoretical performance guarantees. To address these limitations, we introduce a new formulation of the MFBO problem as a fused Gaussian Process bandit and develop a corresponding Fused Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound (FGP-UCB) algorithm. Our approach accurately predicts the high-fidelity function by fusing multi-fidelity observations through an autoregressive Gaussian Process model and explicitly quantifies the uncertainty arising from parameter estimation across fidelity levels. The proposed method also provides theoretical simple-regret guarantees, overcoming a key limitation of existing MFBO algorithms that lack provable performance bounds. Effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated via both theoretical analysis and empirical studies.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) approach using a fused Gaussian Process bandit framework, specifically the Fused Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound (FGP-UCB) algorithm. It leverages autoregressive Gaussian Process models to combine multi-fidelity observations and quantify uncertainty across fidelity levels.
data_sources: The paper does not specify particular financial data sources but broadly refers to expensive black-box functions and lower-fidelity models, which could in principle include financial models or trading strategy evaluations.
alpha_potential: The methodology could potentially optimize trading strategies or portfolio allocations where high-fidelity evaluations (e.g., backtests) are expensive, and lower-fidelity approximations (e.g., simplified models or partial data) can provide informative signals at lower cost.
title_cn: 基于融合高斯过程的多保真度贝叶斯优化框架
summary_cn: 该论文提出了一种多保真度贝叶斯优化框架，通过融合高斯过程与置信上界算法（FGP-UCB），在量化交易中可用于高效优化高成本策略评估（如复杂回测）与低成本近似模型（如简化策略）之间的权衡，提升策略开发效率。

title: Soft Decentralized Expected SARSA: Equilibrium Selection via Gradual Adaptation
summary: We introduce Soft Decentralized Expected SARSA (SDES), a modification of Decentralized Q-learning in which agents maintain persistent exploration and update their acting Q-values gradually rather than switching directly to newly learned best responses when updating. We prove convergence to $\epsilon$-greedy Nash equilibria in weakly acyclic stochastic games for sufficiently large batch sizes. We then show, in the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with memory, that soft updating can reshape basins of attraction without changing the equilibrium set. In the deterministic limit, we derive analytical basin bounds governed by the Q-value differences between actions in the target policies and show that reducing the policy learning rate can favor either cooperative or competitive equilibria. These results suggest that soft updating is not merely a stabilization device but also a mechanism of equilibrium selection in decentralized learning.
core_methodology: Soft Decentralized Expected SARSA (SDES), a modified version of Decentralized Q-learning with persistent exploration and gradual Q-value updates
data_sources: Simulated environments (e.g., repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with memory)
alpha_potential: Potential for equilibrium selection in multi-agent settings, but practical financial applications are unclear

title: What Must LLM Agents Communicate? From Information Loss to Communication Failures
summary: When evidence is distributed across LLM agents, a team may collectively possess all the information needed for a decision yet fail to use it effectively. What must agents communicate for accurate joint predictions, and when does interaction help? We study three requirements for effective communication: sufficiency of the information conveyed, selection of relevant evidence, and utilization of received information. Drawing on information theory and communication complexity, we develop a framework that combines theoretical benchmarks with controlled experiments and message-level analyses. We find that local probability reports can discard essential information, with theoretical information loss closely matching observed performance penalties. Query-first interaction improves predictions when relevant evidence depends on a private query, but compact one-shot representations can eliminate this advantage. Even when sufficient information is communicated, agents may fail to select or use it correctly. Together, these findings distinguish fundamental communication limits from failures in how LLM agents communicate and use information.
core_methodology: The paper studies communication and information utilization among LLM agents, focusing on information theory and communication complexity.
data_sources: Not explicitly mentioned, but likely synthetic or controlled experimental data.
alpha_potential: The paper's insights into agent communication could indirectly inform multi-agent trading systems, though not directly applicable.

title: Understanding Failure Patterns in LLM-Based Mathematical Optimization Modeling
summary: Industrial optimization involves complex constraints, making optimization modeling difficult to automate. Large language models (LLMs) have been explored for generating optimization models from natural language, but their reliability in end-to-end settings remains limited, often producing non-executable, infeasible, or feasible but incorrect solutions. In this work, we study failure modes in LLM-based optimization modeling by decomposing the process into three components: mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge, and constructing datasets that target each aspect. Using these datasets, we analyze how different components relate to errors and find that they are associated with different types of failure, although these relationships are not always strong or consistent. Furthermore, while combining these components improves execution reliability, feasible but incorrect solutions remain the dominant failure mode, suggesting a remaining gap between executability and correctness. These findings highlight limitations of current dataset designs and suggest the importance of data that better capture constraint completeness and formulation accuracy to enhance reliability.
core_methodology: The paper decomposes LLM-based optimization modeling into mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge components, analyzing their failure patterns.
data_sources: The study uses constructed datasets targeting each component of the optimization modeling process.
alpha_potential: Limited direct alpha potential; primarily focuses on reliability of LLMs in optimization, which could indirectly benefit portfolio optimization if reliability issues are addressed.

title: The Danger of Double Precision: Working Precision as a Hidden Constraint in Gaussian Process Maximum Likelihood
summary: Gaussian process (GP) hyperparameters are routinely fitted by maximizing the marginal likelihood in IEEE double precision, although for smooth kernels and noiseless data the covariance matrix is often more ill conditioned than double precision can resolve. For a squared-exponential kernel on a design with a Bayesian-optimization cluster, refits over a range of significand widths, judged against a high-precision reference, show that the double-precision fit is a different model and that fits converge only once the width exceeds the base-2 logarithm of the covariance condition number, about 70 bits. Cholesky failure acts as an implicit conditioning constraint, caused mostly by rounding of the kernel entries; the constrained solution predicted from the working precision alone is within 20% of the best Powell fits at five of the six precisions from 40 to 64 bits, with a local expansion proved for the idealized problem. Across 43 kernels, designs and problem settings, including negative controls that double precision already resolves, the bits needed follow the log condition number at the reference optimum plus a tolerance-dependent offset, and at the loosest tolerance double precision suffices for the Matern 1.5 kernel but not for the squared-exponential kernel on clustered designs. Double-precision hyperparameters overstate the posterior standard deviation near the design cluster and, on a quadratic objective whose likelihood heads to the flat limit, stall closed-loop active learning. Promoting the whole likelihood to 80 significand bits recovers the reference accuracy on every fixed design tested, whereas a fixed jitter trades failures for a posterior bias.
core_methodology: The paper explores the limitations of using double precision in Gaussian Process (GP) hyperparameter optimization, particularly for ill-conditioned covariance matrices, and suggests higher precision arithmetic as a solution.
data_sources: No specific financial data is mentioned; the methodology is theoretical and applies to general GP models, which could be adapted for financial data.
alpha_potential: The findings could indirectly benefit quantitative trading by improving the accuracy of GP-based models used for prediction or anomaly detection, but the direct link to trading strategies is weak.

title: Don't Waste the Population: Post-Anneal Refinement for Combinatorial Optimization
summary: Parallel annealers generate diverse candidate solutions; yet, conventional post-processing typically refines only the best, leaving much of the population's potential untapped. We introduce Iterative Path-Relinking Polish (I-PRP), a deterministic, training-free method that exploits this diversity to discover better solutions without modifying the underlying annealing process. I-PRP selects promising candidates, explores cost-guided paths between locally optimized solutions, and refines intermediate states to uncover better local minima. Newly discovered improvements are iteratively incorporated into the population, enabling further exploration. We theoretically guarantee that I-PRP never degrades solution quality relative to conventional single-candidate polishing on the same population and converges in finitely many iterations. Experiments across challenging combinatorial optimization benchmarks, including MaxCut, MaxClique, and graph coloring, demonstrate substantial improvements in several instances. Paired evaluations confirm non-degradation, while matched-runtime comparisons show that exploiting existing population diversity can outperform additional annealing. These results establish I-PRP as an effective and reliable refinement strategy for parallel annealing.
core_methodology: Deterministic, training-free method (Iterative Path-Relinking Polish - I-PRP) that refines diverse candidate solutions generated by parallel annealers.
data_sources: Benchmark problems in combinatorial optimization (MaxCut, MaxClique, graph coloring).
alpha_potential: Limited direct alpha potential; focused on improving solutions in combinatorial optimization, which could indirectly benefit portfolio optimization or trade execution.

title: Post-Training Policy Replication for Strategy-Following Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning across Team Sizes
summary: Although multi-agent deep reinforcement learning enables coordinated behavior, aligning it with managerial intent remains difficult due to complex agent interactions. Although the strategy-following distributed attentional actor architecture (sfDA7-X) improves controllability via regional instructions, instruction combinations scale exponentially with team and instruction sizes, leading to prohibitive training costs and poor transferability. To reduce this computational cost, we introduce a team-size-independent observation architecture and reconstruct collective behavior by replicating a single trained policy across agents in teams of different sizes, thereby eliminating the need to train from scratch. Additionally, we evaluate warm-start retraining by initializing policy networks with a pre-trained policy to significantly lower computational overhead. In an object collection game, a policy trained in a four-agent team is deployed to teams of three to eight agents. Experiments demonstrate that training with the proposed aggregated observation matrix achieves performance comparable to that of the baseline method, sfDA7-X. Furthermore, policy replication preserves performance without substantial degradation in three- and five-agent teams, and warm-start retraining outperforms training from scratch while reducing required training episodes by up to 90%. Deployments to six- and eight-agent teams further confirm effective spatial region allocation following given instructions. These results demonstrate that the proposed method enables zero-shot collective behavior reconstruction via policy replication.
core_methodology: Policy replication and warm-start retraining in multi-agent deep reinforcement learning
data_sources: Simulated environment (object collection game)
alpha_potential: Potential for scalable multi-agent trading strategies, but requires significant adaptation to financial markets

title: Budget, Readout or Reasoning? Where Small Reasoning Models Lose Value in Auction Bidding
summary: Ad platforms and marketplaces show bidders a bid landscape, the estimated chance of winning at each candidate bid, and increasingly let agents built on reasoning language models choose the bid. We give six open reasoning models of 4B to 14B parameters such landscapes, with win curves from eBay closing prices and from a simulated advertising market (AuctionNet), and score their bids on held-out auctions against an exact calculator. Because the agent is handed the estimates, the lost value can be split by cause. Two failures belong to the models. They pass over the best option even when the values written in their own trace already rank it first, and their wrong answers lean toward the highest bid on the menu. The lean is about the bid's size, not its place in the list, and it survives sampling. At 768 forced tokens on eBay, under pay-your-bid pricing, the wrong answers cost bidders 7-17% of the surplus the calculator's bids earn. Arithmetic errors are rare. Two further losses come from operator choices. A token cap cuts traces short: allowed to stop on their own within 4,096 tokens, five models recover 91-100% of the calculator's lead over a model that does no reasoning. Asking for the answer while the reasoning block is still open misreads it: closing the block first lifts the weakest model from 42% to 84% on eBay and from 24% to 81% on AuctionNet. Finally, an audit that flags bids disagreeing with the trace's own numbers, and overrides them with the calculator's bid, raises the share of the calculator's lead recovered at 768 forced tokens from 42-85% to 84-100% on eBay under nested cross-validation, and the same reader settings transfer from eBay to AuctionNet.
core_methodology: Evaluation of reasoning language models in auction bidding scenarios using win curves from eBay and simulated advertising markets.
data_sources: eBay closing prices and simulated advertising market data (AuctionNet)
alpha_potential: Limited direct application to trading; focuses on bid optimization in auctions which may have tangential relevance to market microstructure or algorithmic bidding strategies.

title: EXPOSURE: Explaining Sources of Uncertainty in Reinforcement Learning
summary: Shapley values in reinforcement learning are used to explain which observation features drive an agent's behavior and expected return, but not its certainty. Explaining certainty requires understanding how observation features influence different sources of return uncertainty, and Shapley values need the agent's prediction for every subset of visible features. We propose EXPOSURE, which uses one mask-aware belief network for both action selection and Shapley explanations. It explains the variance of the return, split into an observational part due to missing features and an inherent part due to the environment's own randomness, and the entropy of its belief over the masked features. In tic-tac-toe and Minesweeper, where exact Shapley values are computable, EXPOSURE gives more accurate explanations of expected return and its uncertainty, while uniquely explaining belief uncertainty.
core_methodology: EXPOSURE uses Shapley values and a mask-aware belief network to explain sources of uncertainty in reinforcement learning, focusing on observational and inherent uncertainties.
data_sources: The paper uses simulated environments like tic-tac-toe and Minesweeper for validation, not real financial data.
alpha_potential: Potential to enhance understanding of model uncertainty in RL-based trading systems, but lacks direct financial application.

title: Resilience Analysis Through Automated Stage Identification and Quantitative Assessment
summary: This paper introduced an ML-based approach, designed to be domain- and threat-agnostic, for automated recognition of PARA (Plan/Prepare, Absorb, Recover, Adapt) resilience stages in system-performance time series, enabling subsequent quantitative resilience analysis across different systems. We investigate four ML models for resilience stage recognition: Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). We then use the ML models' predictions to quantify system resilience by computing corresponding resilience metrics from system-performance data observed before, during, and after disruptive events. We evaluate the proposed approach using datasets from two distinct operational domain network systems and an airport transportation system, demonstrating its domain-agnostic applicability to resilience assessment. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of resilience stage classification, with the best F1-scores ranging from 74.3% to 99.4% across all resilience stages. The overall resilience metrics R_t and RL are estimated, with the best models' MAPE ranging from 0.35-0.82% on IEEE 802.11 and LTE to 1.65-9.56% for the airport. These results provide a basis for threat-agnostic resilience analysis of complex engineering systems, enabling further assessment of how effectively a system withstands, absorbs, and recovers from disruptive events and stress conditions.
core_methodology: ML-based approach using Random Forest, SVM, LightGBM, and XGBoost for automated recognition of resilience stages in system-performance time series.
data_sources: Datasets from operational domain network systems and an airport transportation system.
alpha_potential: Limited direct application to trading; potential in understanding market resilience or stress periods, but not directly actionable for alpha generation.

title: When the Proxy Is Wrong: Mismatch-Corrected Bandits for Adaptive Data Sampling
summary: Data allocation methods often use a small proxy model to select training data for a larger target model. However, this proxy can rank data differently from the target, leading to suboptimal training performance. To address this problem, we model the mismatch between the proxy and target models and incorporate it into the allocation decision. To do so, the problem is cast as a multi-fidelity bandit, where each arm is a data intervention. The proxy reward is observed every round, whereas the target reward is revealed only on rare audits of the same update. These paired observations identify arm-wise mismatches without assuming a shared offset or preservation of rankings. Mismatch-corrected bandits correct the proxy with paired residuals, audit only uncertain decisions, and pace the audit budget over training. From a theoretical viewpoint, we prove a regret decomposition and lower bounds under stationarity. These bounds show that proxy-only allocation can incur linear regret and that a minimum number of paired audits is necessary. Under abrupt changes, using the audit budget early can also incur linear regret. A sliding-window policy that spreads audits over training achieves regret of order $\sqrt{\Gamma_T T\log T}$ where $\Gamma_T$ denotes the number of change points. Experimentally, we test the approach in a closed-loop proof of concept on CivilComments-WILDS, where BERT-Small guides the training of BERT-Large. Mismatch correction improves worst-group accuracy over a target-only policy with the same target-model budget. Spreading audits over training improves worst-group accuracy by 6.3 to 10.5 percentage points at the same audit count.
core_methodology: Multi-fidelity bandits for mismatch correction between proxy and target models in data allocation
data_sources: Text data (CivilComments-WILDS), but methodology could theoretically be applied to financial time series
alpha_potential: Potential application in adaptive sampling of financial data streams where proxy models (e.g., lightweight versions) could guide allocation of computational resources to more important data points

title: Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks
summary: The emerging field of weight space learning has demonstrated the potential to enable metanetworks, i.e. models that process neural network (NN) data, to support several steps of the machine learning lifecycle, from model optimisation to evaluation and adaptation. However, this potential has yet to materialise beyond small-scale MLPs or CNNs: most current models, including message-passing based graph metanetworks (GMNs), operate exclusively at the finest level of granularity, processing every neuron and weight of the input model. Their cost therefore scales with the number of parameters. Yet NNs are inherently organised hierarchically, with neurons forming layers and layers forming blocks and modules. Additionally, several of their properties, such as Lipschitz upper bounds and generalisation measures, are compositions of layer- and block-level quantities. To incorporate this inductive bias, we introduce Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks (H-GMNs), which leverage the input architecture's hierarchy to coarsen and refine the graph using permutation-symmetry-preserving pooling and un-pooling layers. Further, we extend H-GMNs to Transformers by introducing a graph construction that preserves permutation symmetries and enables multi-level pooling. Our evaluation includes new ResNet-18, ViT and varying ViT model zoos of up to 86M parameters, on tasks spanning model evaluation (an analytic Lipschitz bound proxy, generalisation and robustness prediction), testing (backdoor detection) and editing (pruning). Experimental results show that, compared to non-equivariant alternatives and flat GMNs, H-GMNs are markedly more sample-efficient, and their cost remains nearly constant as metanetwork depth grows, allowing deeper and more expressive processing where flat GMNs run out of memory, without compromising accuracy, which in certain cases considerably improves.
core_methodology: Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks (H-GMNs) leveraging NN architecture hierarchy for efficient processing of neural network data, including coarsening and refining graphs with permutation-symmetry-preserving pooling and un-pooling layers.
data_sources: Neural network model zoos (e.g., ResNet-18, ViT, varying ViT models) up to 86M parameters.
alpha_potential: Potential for improving model evaluation, testing, and editing tasks, but direct application to financial data or trading strategies is not evident.

title: Split-RL: Local Conflict Resolution in Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies are often trained by mixing contradictory feedback that is localized in space and time. For example, a robot may prioritize speed in open areas versus precision in tight gaps. We introduce Split-RL, a Gradient Boosting Trees (GBT) algorithm that uses guidance labels to locally isolate these conflicting signals. Standard neural networks (NNs) lack the structural mechanism to do this, as their parameters share feedback from all sources. While GBT provides the inductive bias to explicitly partition the state-space per objective, standard tree-fitting procedures aggregate contradictory gradient signals before they reach the leaves. Split-RL leverages this bias to integrate guidance labels into tree construction, routing these updates into disjoint state-space regions and preventing signal interference. Such labels can arise from heuristics, sensor-derived events, or existing rule-based systems, allowing Split-RL to incorporate rule-derived structure while retaining a learned policy. We theoretically show how early gradient aggregation loses objective-specific information and characterize when the Split-RL score isolates conflicting updates. We focus on constrained RL and offline RL with mixed datasets, each balancing two objectives that conflict locally. Across domains with spatial, rare-event, and temporal conflicts, Split-RL consistently outperforms existing methods by meeting the episodic cost budget while maintaining competitive rewards. In offline settings, Split-RL localizes the tradeoff between imitation and policy improvement, outperforming other methods and achieving near-expert performance across varying dataset sizes.
core_methodology: Split-RL introduces a Gradient Boosting Trees (GBT) algorithm that uses guidance labels to locally isolate conflicting signals in reinforcement learning policies, preventing signal interference.
data_sources: Potentially applicable to any financial datasets where conflicting signals exist, such as mixed frequency data or multi-objective trading strategies.
alpha_potential: The methodology could be adapted to handle conflicting signals in trading strategies, such as balancing short-term and long-term objectives, but the paper does not specifically address financial applications.

title: Evaluating Ensemble Methods for Algorithmic Stability Under Data Perturbations
summary: Standard classification algorithms often exhibit sensitivity near decision boundaries, which can compound instability that already exists from overfitting to a subset of high-influence samples. Ensembling is commonly used to stabilize classifiers, but we show that it can destabilize those that are already stable. The well-established practice of subbagging can yield substantial improvements in stability, as we validate in the cause-of-death classification setting. However, its effect depends on the perturbation level, and for stable classifiers the finite number of bags introduces destabilizing Monte Carlo noise that shrinks only slowly as the number of bags grows. This instability can be mitigated, though, by the recently proposed inflated argmax, which allows for multi-class predictions in ambiguous cases. We further examine the extent to which the Rashomon set, the collection of distinct models that achieve near-optimal predictive performance, can reduce instability by leveraging predictive multiplicity rather than resampling. We find that the Rashomon ensemble can stabilize unstable classifiers, but requires sufficient predictive multiplicity, which is not guaranteed. It is a promising direction, but not currently a general substitute for subbagging. Our results are consistent with an influence equalization interpretation of why these ensemble approaches stabilize unstable classifiers, although their failures on stable classifiers appear to have distinct sources.
core_methodology: Evaluating ensemble methods (subbagging and Rashomon sets) for improving algorithmic stability under data perturbations
data_sources: Cause-of-death classification setting (non-financial)
alpha_potential: Limited direct application to trading; potential theoretical insights into classifier stability that might inform financial prediction models

title: Decision-Focused Learning for Multistage Stochastic Programs, with Application to Power Network Repair Scheduling
summary: Multistage stochastic programs (MSPs) with discrete decisions are hard to solve due to the curse of dimensionality, non-convex value functions, and scenario trees that grow exponentially with the horizon. We develop a decision-focused learning (DFL) framework for MSPs in which a neural network predicts scores for the part of the decision that drives the state transition. Under structural conditions that make this sub-decision enter the stage objective linearly, the network is trained on labels from offline single-scenario problems, using the Fenchel-Young loss with perturbed optimizers, which need only an optimization oracle. We apply the framework to repair scheduling in power networks under stochastic, time-varying component failures, with and without a per-stage repair budget. On a synthetic 5-bus network and on the IEEE 14-bus network at two repair-cost scales, the learned and baseline policies are compared on common evaluation paths. Without the budget, DFL is the cheapest policy on the 5-bus network; on the 14-bus network it does not outperform a near-sighted model-predictive control (MPC) baseline, but it beats repairing every failed component at the higher scale. Under a binding budget, DFL is the cheapest policy evaluated on both networks and at both scales, 14% to 23% below the next-best policy. On the 5-bus network, the mean cost of DFL is 1.7% (without the budget) and 1.8% (with it) above the exact optimum computed by dynamic programming. Within days of computation, sample average approximation yields costlier policies than DFL and the repair-everything heuristic, and stochastic dual dynamic integer programming remains far from convergence. DFL computes its decisions about as fast as the trivial heuristics and orders of magnitude faster than MPC. Since these conditions are not specific to power networks, the framework extends to other MSPs that share this structure.
core_methodology: Decision-focused learning (DFL) framework for multistage stochastic programs, using neural networks to predict scores for decisions driving state transitions, trained with Fenchel-Young loss and perturbed optimizers.
data_sources: Synthetic 5-bus network and IEEE 14-bus network data for power network repair scheduling under stochastic, time-varying component failures.
alpha_potential: Potential for optimizing sequential decision-making under uncertainty, though primarily applied to power networks with limited direct financial application.

title: Backpropagation as Dirac-bracket dynamics of dissipative training
summary: Gradient-based training of a parametric model is the motion of a damped particle in the potential set by the loss. Using the Bateman-Galley doubling of the degrees of freedom, which gives dissipative systems an action principle, we write gradient flow, the heavy-ball method and Nesterov's accelerated gradient method as Hamiltonian systems. We show that, within this Hamiltonian description, backpropagation is Dirac evolution. The activations of a feed-forward network are treated as coordinates of phase space, and the layer equations as constraints. These constraints are second class for every architecture, and Hamilton's equations with the resulting Dirac bracket reproduce training with the exact gradient of the loss, although the Hamiltonian contains only the cost of the network output. The Dirac bracket of an activation with the momenta of the parameters is its Jacobian, the inverse of the constraint matrix contains both the forward and the reverse modes of automatic differentiation, and the errors propagated by backpropagation are the Lagrange multipliers of the layer constraints: the constraint forces of a kinematic chain under the load of the cost. These results hold in the full doubled phase space, not only in the physical limit. The network's part of the constraint algebra is the same for every optimizer, Nesterov's look-ahead adds one layer of momentum-dependent constraints that couple the two copies of the doubled system, and gradient flow is obtained by constructing the Dirac bracket in stages. We confirm these statements numerically to machine precision and train a network by integrating the Dirac flow of its constraints, with no backward pass in the computation.
core_methodology: The paper presents a Hamiltonian system approach to gradient-based training methods, including backpropagation, using the Bateman-Galley doubling of degrees of freedom to describe dissipative systems with an action principle.
data_sources: Theoretical framework applicable to any data used in training parametric models, though no specific financial data is mentioned.
alpha_potential: The methodology could potentially improve optimization in machine learning models used in trading, but the direct application to alpha generation is unclear.

title: Sketching for First Order Method: Efficient Algorithm for Low-Bandwidth Channel and Vulnerability
summary: Sketching, which randomly compresses a large problem into lower dimensions to save runtime and memory, is a fundamental tool in large-scale machine learning. We propose a sketching scheme for first order methods in distributed learning that reduces the communication cost per round between agents, keeps our bound on the total communication no larger than for uncompressed distributed gradient descent, and still guarantees convergence. An agent compresses a gradient of high dimension $d$ with a sketching matrix $R\in\mathbb{R}^{s\times d}$, $s\ll d$, and the receiver maps it back to dimension $d$ with the de-sketching matrix $R^\top$. Using this framework, we develop federated learning algorithms with lower per-round communication. However, such random sketching alone gives no formal privacy guarantee for the local data. We present a gradient-matching attack and prove that, under smoothness and non-degeneracy assumptions on the model, gradient descent on the data finds an input whose sketched gradient matches the observed one, at a linear rate. This input need not be the data, but an attacker that follows a client over several rounds with fresh sketches recovers the data with the same attack, under smoothness and non-degeneracy conditions, and no attack does so from the first $T<m/s$ rounds, where $m$ is the data dimension. As a remedy, we prove that adding Gaussian noise to the gradients makes the algorithm differentially private. This noisy variant still sends only $s$ numbers per client in each round, and for convex and strongly convex objectives it converges at the rates of the noise-free algorithm, up to an additive error term that depends on the privacy level and, in our bounds, grows as $s$ decreases. Our total communication guarantees are proved for the noise-free algorithm. We expect our sketching scheme to extend to other learning settings, and it may be of independent interest.
core_methodology: Sketching technique for compressing and decompressing gradients in distributed learning
data_sources: Not directly specified, likely applicable to various gradient-based optimization tasks
alpha_potential: Potential for reducing communication costs in distributed optimization settings, but no direct financial application

title: Tensor Networks Meet Neural Networks: A Survey and Future Perspectives
summary: Tensor networks (TNs) and neural networks (NNs) are two fundamental data modeling approaches. TNs were introduced to solve the curse of dimensionality in large-scale tensors by converting an exponential number of dimensions to polynomial complexity. As a result, they have attracted significant attention in the fields of quantum physics and machine learning. Meanwhile, NNs have displayed exceptional performance in various applications, e.g., computer vision, natural language processing, and robotics research. Interestingly, although these two types of networks originate from different observations, they are inherently linked through the typical multilinearity structure underlying both TNs and NNs, thereby motivating a significant number of developments regarding combinations of TNs and NNs. In this paper, we refer to these combinations as tensorial neural networks~(TNNs) and present an introduction to TNNs from both data processing and model architecture perspectives. From the data perspective, we explore the capabilities of TNNs in multi-source fusion, multimodal pooling, data compression, multi-task training, and quantum data processing. From the model perspective, we examine TNNs' integration with various architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks, Recurrent Neural Networks, Graph Neural Networks, Transformers, Large Language Models, and Quantum Neural Networks. Furthermore, this survey also explores methods for improving TNNs, examines flexible toolboxes for implementing TNNs, and documents TNN development while highlighting potential future directions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive survey that bridges the connections among NNs and TNs. We provide a curated list of TNNs at https://github.com/tnbar/awesome-tensorial-neural-networks.
core_methodology: Combination of tensor networks and neural networks for data modeling and processing
data_sources: Multi-source, multimodal, and possibly quantum data
alpha_potential: Potential for improved data compression, multi-task training, and integration with various neural network architectures, but direct financial application is unclear

title: Analysis of Variational Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Variational sparse autoencoders (vSAEs) replace a sparse autoencoder's deterministic Top-K mechanism with a sampled Gaussian posterior hypothesized to produce a more robust feature dictionary. To test this, we build permutation comparisons over training seeds for custom analyses, and score two popular benchmarks on one pair of existing checkpoints. When fixing the unit variance and ablating sampling on the vSAE, we find that the gap between the non-sampled vSAE and a Top-K SAE with an L2 activation penalty can be decomposed completely into a set of five implementation details. When we enable sampling and allow the network to learn its own variance, we find that the discrete selection process of Top-K fails when in conjunction with stochastic sampling methods. At the noise scale these models are trained upon, vastly different Top-K feature sets (Jaccard 0.075-0.29, chance 0.067) are found on equal model activations due only to the sampling noise, in two forward passes of one trained model on the same token. Soft methods such as JumpReLU fail to hold their sparsity target as well due to sampling, though under different failure modes. Noise moves its achieved sparsity, and at matched sparsity reconstruction fails to track selection stability (r = -0.55). Ablating the KL loss term recovers only 3.9 percent of the lost reconstruction. The rest is due to sampling.
core_methodology: Variational sparse autoencoders (vSAEs) with sampled Gaussian posteriors compared against traditional Top-K SAEs with L2 activation penalty
data_sources: Not specified (likely general ML benchmarks given the abstract)
alpha_potential: Low immediate applicability - explores theoretical improvements in autoencoder sparsity but lacks clear financial data connections. Potential for feature extraction if adapted to market data

title: TopoPrune: Robust Data Pruning via Unified Latent Space Topology
summary: Geometric data pruning methods, while practical for leveraging pretrained models, are fundamentally unstable. Their reliance on extrinsic geometry renders them highly sensitive to latent space perturbations, causing performance to degrade during cross-architecture transfer or in the presence of feature noise. We introduce TopoPrune, a framework which resolves this challenge by leveraging topology to capture the stable, intrinsic structure of data. TopoPrune operates at two scales, (1) utilizing a topology-aware manifold approximation to establish a global low-dimensional embedding of the dataset. Subsequently, (2) it employs differentiable persistent homology to perform a local topological optimization on the manifold embeddings, ranking samples by their structural complexity. We demonstrate that our unified dual-scale topological approach ensures high accuracy and precision, particularly at significant dataset pruning rates (e.g., 90%). Furthermore, through the inherent stability properties of topology, TopoPrune is (a) exceptionally robust to noise perturbations of latent feature embeddings and (b) demonstrates superior transferability across diverse network architectures. This study demonstrates a promising avenue towards stable and principled topology-based frameworks for robust data-efficient learning.
core_methodology: Topology-aware manifold approximation and differentiable persistent homology for data pruning
data_sources: Generic latent space data, not specific to financial markets
alpha_potential: Potential for improving data efficiency in model training, but no direct financial alpha generation mechanism

title: AESP: A Human-Sovereign Economic Protocol for AI Agents with Privacy-Preserving Settlement
summary: As AI agents increasingly perform economic tasks on behalf of humans, a fundamental tension arises between agent autonomy and human control over financial assets. We present the Agent Economic Sovereignty Protocol (AESP), a layered protocol in which agents transact autonomously at machine speed on crypto-native infrastructure while remaining cryptographically bound to human-defined governance boundaries. AESP enforces the invariant that agents are economically capable but never economically sovereign through five mechanisms: (1) a deterministic eight-check policy engine with tiered escalation; (2) human-in-the-loop review with automatic, explicit, and biometric tiers; (3) EIP-712 dual-signed commitments with escrow; (4) HKDF-based context-isolated privacy with batched consolidation; and (5) an ACE-GF-based cryptographic substrate. We formalize two testable hypotheses on security coverage and latency overhead, and specify a complete evaluation methodology with baselines and ablation design. The protocol is implemented as an open-source TypeScript SDK (208 tests, ten modules) with interoperability via MCP and A2A.
core_methodology: A layered cryptographic protocol for AI agent autonomy with human oversight in economic transactions
data_sources: Crypto-native infrastructure and transaction data
alpha_potential: Limited potential as focus is on governance/control rather than market signal generation

title: Manifold-Matching Autoencoders
summary: Manipulating the structure of data in the latent space of an autoencoder is a long-standing goal of representation learning. We propose a simple regularization, Manifold Matching, that imposes an explicit geometric structure on that latent space. The idea is to take a reference representation R of the data, which need not be the raw input X fed to the network, and to minimize, batch-wise, the mean squared error between the pairwise distances in R and those in the latent space Z. Although the autoencoder still learns to reconstruct X, the shape of its latent space comes to mimic that of R. The objective requires no labels, only reference distances, and because those are scalars, the dimensionality of R is decoupled from that of Z: any reference can guide any bottleneck. Using this single instrument we study how different geometric structures can be imposed on a latent space, comparing against autoencoders built on geometric or topological regularizers. Across fifteen datasets under a shared protocol with statistical testing, the resulting Manifold-Matching Autoencoder (MMAE) matches the global-structure quality of persistence-based autoencoders, statistically tying RTD-AE on distance correlation and triplet accuracy, and stays competitive on the local and topological metrics that other methods lead, at the computational cost of a plain autoencoder: it uses only a batched distance loss, with no persistence computation. We frame MMAE not as a universal winner but as an efficient and controllable regularizer whose reference selects which structure the latent inherits, and which turns any fixed embedding into a reusable out-of-sample encoder. All experiments use a two-dimensional bottleneck.
core_methodology: Manifold-Matching regularization for autoencoders, imposing geometric structure on latent space by matching pairwise distances to a reference representation.
data_sources: General datasets (not finance-specific), with potential applicability to financial time series or alternative data.
alpha_potential: Potential for creating more structured latent representations of financial data, which could aid in feature extraction or anomaly detection.

title: Regret-Oracle Complexity Tradeoffs in Agnostic Online Learning
summary: Agnostic online learning is classically solved via a reduction to the realizable setting, utilizing Littlestone's Standard Optimal Algorithm (SOA) as a base learner. However, the SOA can be computationally intractable to implement even for a single round. To overcome this barrier, recent work in oracle-efficient online learning replaces the SOA with a realizable base learner that accesses the concept class exclusively through an offline empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. While such agnostic learners achieve expected regret $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(\sqrt{T\cdot 2^{\mathcal{O}(d_{\mathrm{LD}})}}\big)$, which is near-optimal in the horizon $T$ for fixed Littlestone dimension $d_{\mathrm{LD}}$, they require $\mathcal{O}\big(T^{2^{\mathcal{O}(d_{\mathrm{LD}})}}\big)$ oracle calls. In this work, we significantly improve this oracle complexity while relying on an even weaker primitive: a weak-consistency oracle, which merely decides whether a given labeled dataset is realizable. At the core of our approach is an adaptive and dynamic agnostic-to-realizable reduction that actively prunes non-realizable label sequences on the fly. By using the VC dimension ($d_{\mathrm{VC}}$) to bound the number of dynamically maintained active paths, our algorithm reduces the total query complexity down to $\mathcal{O}(T^{d_{\mathrm{VC}}+1})$ while perfectly preserving near-optimal expected regret. Crucially, this dynamic pruning also yields a memory reduction over the standard reduction. Furthermore, we formally quantify the regret--oracle complexity tradeoff, providing upper bounds that smoothly interpolate between restricted query budgets and attainable expected regret. We complement these with lower bounds proving that any learner restricted to $Q = o(\sqrt{T})$ queries must suffer an expected regret of $\Omega(T/Q)$.
core_methodology: The paper focuses on improving oracle efficiency in agnostic online learning by using a weak-consistency oracle and dynamic pruning of non-realizable label sequences. It aims to reduce computational complexity while maintaining near-optimal regret bounds.
data_sources: Theoretical datasets or synthetic data used to validate the algorithm's performance in an online learning setting.
alpha_potential: Limited direct alpha potential. The methodology is more relevant to improving computational efficiency in online learning systems rather than generating trading signals or strategies.

title: Hierarchical Two-Stage Framework for Environment-Aware Long-Horizon Vessel Trajectory Prediction
summary: Long-horizon vessel trajectory forecasting under real ocean conditions is critical for collision avoidance, traffic management, and route planning. However, achieving accurate predictions is challenging due to long-range temporal dependencies and dynamic environmental factors such as currents, wind, and waves. To address these issues, we propose a hierarchical two-stage framework that combines a coarse long-term predictor with a grid-aware short-term predictor through a hierarchical fusion mechanism. The short-term branch leverages a Spatio-Temporal Graph Transformer on discretized maritime cells to capture localized dynamics, while the long-term branch encodes overarching navigational intent. An integrated environmental module incorporates oceanographic parameters, including surface currents, wind vectors, and significant wave height, using cross-modal attention and feature-wise modulation for adaptive response to varying sea conditions. Additionally, a learnable Savitzky-Golay smoothing layer enhances temporal coherence in fused trajectories. We evaluate our approach on Australian Craft Tracking System (CTS) data from the North West region, aligned with Copernicus Marine Service products, using a 3-hour input and a 10-hour prediction horizon. Experimental results show that our framework outperforms the state-of-the-art by 25% in Average Displacement Error (ADE) and 17% in Final Displacement Error (FDE). Ablation studies further validate the contribution of each component.
core_methodology: Hierarchical two-stage framework combining long-term intent prediction with short-term localized dynamics using Spatio-Temporal Graph Transformer and environmental feature modulation
data_sources: Australian Craft Tracking System (CTS) data aligned with Copernicus Marine Service products (oceanographic parameters)
alpha_potential: Potential indirect applications in commodity shipping logistics optimization or weather-impacted supply chain forecasting

title: Global linear convergence of entropy-regularized softmax policy gradient beyond tabular MDPs
summary: We study the global convergence of policy gradient for infinite-horizon entropy-regularized Markov decision processes (MDPs) with continuous state and action spaces. We consider log-linear softmax policies with linear function approximation, which extend the tabular softmax parameterization while retaining a tractable policy class. Under $Q^\pi_\tau$-realizability up to a state-dependent baseline for the regularized state-action value function, we establish a non-uniform Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) inequality for two different feature regimes. The non-uniformity arises through degeneracy of the state-averaged Fisher information matrix in the first feature regime and the uncentered feature second-moment matrix in the second. In both regimes we prove that these non-uniform constants can be bounded uniformly from below along the gradient flow. For full-affine-span features, we prove radial unboundedness of the KL regularizer and show that the state averaged smallest eigenvalue of the Fisher information matrix remains bounded below by an initialization-dependent positive constant. For simplex-valued features, we prove an analogous radial unboundedness result in the subspace orthogonal to the one vector and obtain an initialization dependent lower bound for the state averaged smallest eigenvalue of the uncentered second-moment matrix. These results imply global linear convergence of the regularized objective along the gradient flow, i.e., suboptimality decaying as $\mathcal{O}(e^{-Ct})$ for some $C>0$. Our analysis complements the global convergence theory of entropy-regularized softmax policy gradient beyond the tabular setting of Agarwal et al. (2020); Bhandari and Russo (2024); Mei et al. (2020).
core_methodology: Entropy-regularized softmax policy gradient with linear function approximation in continuous state and action spaces
data_sources: Not specified (theoretical MDPs)
alpha_potential: Potential theoretical foundation for reinforcement learning in portfolio optimization or execution strategies, but requires significant adaptation to real market data

title: A Graph Signal Processing Perspective on Numerical Sequence Representations in LLM In-Context Learning
summary: Pretrained large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated in-context learning (ICL) capabilities for numerical inference over sequences serialized as text. Prior work has identified and characterized this form of numerical inference primarily through output-level evaluations such as prediction error. However, how numerical information is organized within LLM representations remains much less understood. To study this internal organization, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective in which attention induces a weighted graph over tokens, while token hidden states define signals on its nodes. Quantitative graph-spectral diagnostics and qualitative token-graph visualizations reveal that representations become more clearly differentiated by input dynamical complexity as context length increases. Simpler inputs produce attention-induced token graphs with stronger global connectivity and smoother, spectrally concentrated hidden-state signals, whereas more complex inputs produce more localized graphs and hidden-state signals with broader spectral support and greater high-frequency energy. These diagnostics and visualizations offer an interpretable view of the internal structure associated with numerical ICL, beyond what output-level prediction error alone reveals. Together, these findings point to systematic, context-dependent internal signatures associated with numerical ICL that are qualitatively conserved across model families.
core_methodology: The paper adopts a graph signal processing perspective to analyze how numerical information is organized within LLM representations during in-context learning, using attention mechanisms and token hidden states.
data_sources: The paper does not specify particular financial data sources; it focuses on numerical sequences serialized as text within LLMs.
alpha_potential: The methodology could potentially help in understanding how LLMs process numerical financial data sequences, but the direct application to alpha generation is not clear and would require significant adaptation.

title: Replay, Don't Resample: Off-Policy Consolidation of Long-Horizon RL Experts
summary: Frontier post-training follows a common recipe: train one expert per domain with reinforcement learning (RL), then consolidate the experts into one model via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Such consolidation is expensive: the student samples in every environment again, an expert scores every sampled token, and the student inherits the drift of the final experts. Yet we argue that the experts' RL runs have already produced what consolidation needs: rollouts with their sampling probabilities and rewards, in the order the experts learned from them. We propose multi-expert replay policy distillation (MRPD), which replays these training logs through the student in the experts' order. At each step, the policy gradient is recomputed on these scored trajectories, and the final experts' distributions are distilled at the logged prefixes. Following the experts' own trajectory reduces the training-inference mismatch and keeps the student within the clip range, so the replay is off-policy in origin but quasi-on-policy throughout consolidation. MRPD samples nothing and calls no environment or reward model: the trainer is the sole process, and consolidating the experts costs only about a seventh of the compute used to train them. On three long-horizon agentic domains (reasoning, search and SQL), MRPD yields the best student model, substantially outperforming online RL baselines, and surpassing MOPD from the same experts at a fraction of MOPD's cost. Our analysis on the same logs shows that the replayed trajectories carry most of the gain, and that both the policy gradient and the distillation term add to it. Most interestingly, the order of the logs matters more than their amount or rewards, suggesting that expert training logs are a curriculum, not a data mixture.
core_methodology: Off-policy reinforcement learning consolidation through multi-expert replay policy distillation (MRPD)
data_sources: Training logs from expert RL runs (including rollouts, sampling probabilities, and rewards)
alpha_potential: Potential for improving reinforcement learning models in trading by efficiently consolidating multiple expert policies without additional sampling

title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: A Statistical Perspective
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a central framework for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. Despite its practical success, RLHF raises fundamental statistical questions because it relies on noisy, subjective, and heterogeneous feedback to learn reward models and optimize policies. This survey provides a statistical perspective on RLHF, focusing primarily on LLM alignment. We introduce the main components of RLHF, including supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and policy optimization, and relate them to familiar statistical concepts such as the Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model, latent utility estimation, active learning, experimental design, and uncertainty quantification. We review methods for learning reward functions from pairwise preference data and for optimizing policies through both two-stage RLHF pipelines and emerging one-stage approaches such as direct preference optimization. We further discuss recent extensions including reinforcement learning from AI feedback, inference-time algorithms, and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, as well as benchmark datasets, evaluation protocols, and open-source frameworks that support RLHF research. We conclude by highlighting open challenges in RLHF.
core_methodology: Survey of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), including supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and policy optimization, with statistical perspectives like the Bradley-Terry-Luce model and active learning.
data_sources: Human feedback, pairwise preference data, benchmark datasets.
alpha_potential: Limited direct alpha potential as it focuses on LLM alignment rather than financial markets. Indirect potential via improved AI decision-making in trading systems.

title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for Reinforcement Learning Under a Generative Model
