summary: Reinforcement learning is a subfield of machine learning that studies how an agent interacts with an environment in order to extract as large a reward as possible. A standard approach to study such interaction is through Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) and the task of choosing an optimal policy---a function that tells the agent which action to take. In this work, we study two types of time-dependent MDP---finite-horizon and infinite-horizon discounted---and propose new quantum algorithms for computing approximate optimal policies. Our quantum algorithms are based on a new combination of standard value iteration and quantum subroutines like quantum mean estimation and quantum maximum finding, overall enhanced with techniques from sample-optimal classical algorithms. Our resulting query complexities improve upon previous works, thus approaching already established quantum lower bounds.
core_methodology: Quantum algorithms for reinforcement learning based on value iteration, quantum mean estimation, and quantum maximum finding
data_sources: Not specified (theoretical framework)
alpha_potential: Potential for faster policy computation in dynamic environments, but quantum hardware constraints limit practical deployment

title: The Gradient Difference Induced by Detaching the Denominator in QK Normalization
summary: QK normalization divides each query and key by its own RMS norm before the attention scores are computed. Treating this denominator as a constant during backpropagation leaves the forward pass unchanged but alters the parameter gradients. We derive a closed form for the difference between the gradient under this detached rule and the gradient under the standard rule. For a single token, this difference is parallel to the token's own query; it changes only the query norm and has no first-order effect after normalization. The queries, however, are computed by a projection matrix $W_Q$ shared across all tokens. The gradient difference on $W_Q$ therefore equals $W_Q$ right-multiplied by a weighted second moment of the inputs, and it decomposes exactly into three components: a radial component that changes only the norm of $W_Q$, a tangential component that changes the query directions of other tokens, and an upstream component that changes the gradient passed to earlier layers. Under AdamW, the radial component drives $W_Q$ to a larger equilibrium norm and reduces its angular update per step. Paired experiments on a small Transformer language model are consistent with this analysis. Detaching the query denominator consistently raises the test loss, and the gap persists across hardware, evaluation datasets and learning rates. All three components remain non-negligible throughout training, with the tangential component the largest. Norm growth and the smaller angular update appear only on the detached projection matrix, while the other projection matrix is essentially unchanged. With a learnable scale, however, we observe no resolvable loss gap.
core_methodology: The paper examines a gradient difference in QK normalization in Transformers when detaching the denominator during backpropagation, analyzing its impact on learning dynamics.
data_sources: Not specified (likely synthetic or general language model training data as implied by 'Transformer language model' in abstract)
alpha_potential: Minimal direct applicability. The theoretical analysis of gradient behavior in attention mechanisms might indirectly inform Transformer-based market prediction models.

title: SOC-Net: Second-Order-Cone-Constrained Neural Networks
summary: In many applications, neural networks must learn input-output maps that respect prior knowledge such as physical laws, safety requirements, and operating limits. These requirements constrain which outputs are admissible for a given input and often admit second-order cone (SOC) representations, including norm bounds and robust linear inequalities. Examples in control include friction cones, thrust bounds, and input-robust control barrier function (CBF) conditions. However, existing approaches to enforcing general input-dependent SOC constraints require a conic solver, an iterative scheme whose feasibility depends on convergence, or an interior feasible point for each input. We propose SOC-Net, a neural network architecture that enforces input-dependent SOC constraints by construction for every input, even outside the training distribution. SOC-Net projects an affine lifting of the backbone output onto the reachable slice of a fixed product of Lorentz cones and maps the correction back to the output space. For separable constraints, this projection splits into one projection per cone, and each is available in closed form or reduces to a single scalar equation, regardless of the cone dimension. We prove that SOC-Net retains the expressive power of the backbone network under regularity conditions and accommodates end-to-end training by standard backpropagation with an explicit Jacobian. Experiments on contact force allocation with friction constraints and 3-D obstacle avoidance with an input-robust CBF demonstrate that SOC-Net satisfies the constraints at every evaluated input, with lower evaluation latency than the tested solver-based and iterative baselines.
core_methodology: Neural network architecture enforcing input-dependent second-order cone constraints
data_sources: Not specified in abstract (likely synthetic or robotics/control datasets)
alpha_potential: Potentially useful for portfolio optimization under convex constraints, but no direct trading application demonstrated

title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning with State-Dependent Foresight for Human Decision-Making
summary: Computational modeling of behavior represents individuals with a model fitted to their observed behavior and characterizes them through its parameters. Naturalistic tasks incorporate the complexity of real environments and yield high-dimensional behavioral trajectories. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) infers the latent reward function underlying these trajectories. Standard IRL, however, assumes effectively infinite-horizon planning, whereas human foresight is both bounded and state-dependent. Here we introduce SC-AIRL (State-Conditional Adversarial IRL), which builds these two cognitive properties into the planner. Per-depth policies share one reward but differ in how far ahead they sum it explicitly. A state-conditional router mixes them according to the current state. Across held-out episodes in pedestrian crossing and highway overtaking tasks, SC-AIRL improves imitation over Standard AIRL, raising top-1 accuracy from 0.549 to 0.647 and from 0.629 to 0.718, respectively, while more closely reproducing participant behavior in rollouts. Inferred planning depth correlates with self-reported anxiety and motor impulsivity. SC-AIRL thus reproduces human behavior more closely than Standard AIRL while providing an interpretable, model-derived measure of state-dependent foresight.
core_methodology: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) with state-dependent foresight modeling for human decision-making
data_sources: Behavioral trajectories from pedestrian crossing and highway overtaking tasks
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability to financial markets; potential for modeling trader behavior but requires significant adaptation

title: Distractor-Robust Reinforcement Learning via Variational Bisimulation
summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) promises data efficiency and generalization, but typical reconstruction-based objectives encourage models to waste representational capacity on task-irrelevant distractors. We introduce VIBES (Variational Inference for Bisimulation-based Encoded States), a new objective that replaces pixel reconstruction with an adversarial term, which enforces that latent states suffice to predict both rewards and the next latent state. We show that this objective measures how far the encoder is from reward and dynamics sufficiency, and that whenever exact sufficiency is attainable, its global optima induce bisimulation relations on histories. Combined with a fixed-capacity latent bottleneck, this encourages latent states to retain task-relevant information while discarding irrelevant variation. Our method serves as a drop-in replacement for Dreamer's model-learning component, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Distracting Control Suite, and extends to visually complex manipulation in Realistic ManiSkill. Unlike prior approaches, it does not rely on image-specific augmentations and applies equally well to high-dimensional vector-state tasks, demonstrated on a 100-link swimmer robot. Finally, latent-space analyses (UMAP embeddings and nearest-neighbor probes) confirm that the learned representations are sensitive to task-relevant structure while invariant to distractors.
core_methodology: Uses Variational Inference for Bisimulation-based Encoded States (VIBES) to focus on task-relevant information in reinforcement learning by discarding irrelevant distractors.
data_sources: High-dimensional sensory data (e.g., pixels from visual inputs or vector-state tasks).
alpha_potential: Potential to improve learning efficiency in tasks where irrelevant data (noise) can obscure important signals, but direct financial application is unclear.

title: A Causal Energy Prior for Learning Directed Acyclic Graphs
summary: Bayesian learning of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) has long relied on non- or weakly informative priors, on the assumption that the information needed for an informative one is rarely available. In genetics and systems biology, annotation databases now make it possible to assemble a prior DAG before learning from data. Existing informative priors are local: they score a DAG arc by arc and cannot encode how interventions propagate along its paths. Thus, we propose the local-global energy prior (LGE), a Gibbs distribution over DAGs whose energy combines a local divergence from the prior DAG, the Structural Hamming Distance, and a causal one, the Structural Intervention Distance. We derive rules to calibrate its decay and the weight of the two divergences from the prior DAG alone. We quantify how much prior mass stays on the true DAG, and how much data overturn the prior, when the prior DAG is partially incorrect. In simulations, LGE improves both the structural accuracy of maximum a posteriori DAGs and the fit of the corresponding Bayesian networks to the true distribution over non- and weakly informative priors, even when half of the arcs of the prior DAG are wrong. We also showcase LGE on a gene regulatory network learned from single-cell kidney data.
core_methodology: Bayesian learning of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) using a local-global energy prior (LGE) that combines local and causal divergences.
data_sources: Genetics and systems biology annotation databases, single-cell kidney data.
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability to quantitative trading; potential indirect value in improving causal inference models for financial networks.

title: Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization Beyond $1/e$ with Feasible Gradient Queries
summary: We study adversarial online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed sets $K\subseteq[0,1]^d$ when gradients may be queried only at feasible points. The online approximation coefficients $4/9$ (Aggarwal and Lu) and $2\sqrt{3}-3\approx 0.4641$ (Aggarwal and Du) rely on queries along chains that start from the all-ones vector and leave $K$. With every query in $K$, the best known coefficient was $1/e$. We give an online algorithm with coefficient $0.4013$ that, in each round, plays a random action, queries one gradient at a point of $K$, and makes one projection. Its expected approximate regret is $O(RB(1+R)\sqrt{T})$, where $R\le\sqrt{d}$ bounds the norm of points of $K$ and $B$ bounds the gradient norm on $K$. For a budget $\sum_i x_i\le k$, the bound is $O(kB\sqrt{T})$. The algorithm keeps a state $x\in K$, and the analysis applies the coordinate-chain comparison of Aggarwal and Lu inside the box $[0,x]$, which keeps every query feasible. A second comparison, along a path from $0$ in the direction $x$, cancels the extra terms that the box creates. Because the queries are feasible, they can be played, which gives regret $O(T^{2/3})$ under semi-bandit feedback and $O(T^{4/5})$ under bandit feedback with bounded values. Unbiased stochastic gradients with bounded second moment keep the $\sqrt{T}$ rate, and on a fixed function the algorithm attains $0.4013\,\mathrm{OPT}-\varepsilon$ in expectation with $O(1+R^2(1+R)^2B^2/\varepsilon^2)$ feasible gradient queries.
core_methodology: Online non-monotone DR-submodular maximization with feasible gradient queries
data_sources: Not specified, possibly simulated or theoretical data
alpha_potential: Limited direct application; theoretical approach to optimization over convex sets that might be adapted for portfolio allocation problems

title: Agent Calibration under Deployment Change: Acceptance Contracts, Trajectory Repair, and Adaptation Costs
summary: An agent can remain operational after a model, tool, or user-context change while losing capabilities required at its destination. We define agent calibration as qualification against a versioned deployment contract. The contract specifies basic capabilities and end-to-end reachability, technical and professional precision, and acceptance by intended users. For each requirement, a source-to-destination map records what must be preserved, transformed, added, or retired. Experts supply benchmarks, positive and negative examples, annotated trajectories, and cost limits. These instruments guide changes to prompts and context, tool calls and other harness settings, or an external compact policy while the foundation model remains frozen. Candidate revisions are evaluated against fixed acceptance criteria using independent evidence. We compare the costs of maintaining a harness with and without an external policy, including annotation, training, serving, review, and rework. Three diagnostic audits illustrate the limits of aggregate scores. On a 100-item intent task, each model solved cases the other missed. In a 60-record synthetic financial reporting fixture, five records passed a numeric proxy but failed the reporting contract. In a target-only WebMall snapshot, quota interruptions affected 132 of 171 attempts. These observations motivate paired reruns, checkpoint replay, and separate measurement of repaired and newly failed cases. We specify controlled experiments to test whether calibration increases accepted deliveries at a given cost.
core_methodology: Agent calibration against versioned deployment contracts, involving benchmarks, examples, annotated trajectories, and cost limits.
data_sources: Synthetic financial reporting fixture, WebMall snapshot, and intent task records.
alpha_potential: Low potential; focuses on maintaining agent capabilities post-deployment rather than generating trading signals or strategies.

title: FinAutoRubric: Expert-Guided Automatic Rubric Generation for Evaluating Financial Research Agents
summary: Evaluating finance research agents requires rubrics that reflect expert standards and fix the values correct as of an information cutoff. Expert-reviewed finance benchmarks rely on fixed, per-item rubrics, which are costly to extend and cannot encode each institution's own standard. In FinAutoRubric, experts specify reusable evaluation guidance, while agents and code carry out query-specific rubric generation, review, and validation. This expert guidance governs every agent, as prompts and as rules that code enforces, and a Task Bank of reusable criteria carries it across tasks. In long-horizon loops that follow the expert guidance, a writer agent researches every expected value and a reviewer agent verifies it, and failures escalate to a human. On three expert-authored finance benchmarks, its rubrics track expert scoring as closely as the strongest evaluated generator while stating the expert rubric's expected value for more criteria, their scores agree with human grading, and in-house analysts prefer them in a blind review. The released 100-query FinAutoRubric Benchmark, built from in-house analysts' key questions across 78 tasks and eight asset classes, shows that rubrics from an earlier model generation still leave headroom for a later one.
core_methodology: Expert-guided automatic rubric generation for evaluating financial research agents
data_sources: Expert-authored finance benchmarks and in-house analysts' key questions
alpha_potential: Limited direct alpha potential; focuses on evaluation rather than signal generation

title: InterQ-RL: Interaction-Aware Correction of Execution Mismatch in Quantized Agentic RL
summary: Multi-turn agent reinforcement learning (RL) relies on long closed-loop rollouts, making generation and KV-cache costs a major bottleneck. Quantized rollout reduces these costs, but its low-precision executor also serves as the behavior policy and can induce execution mismatch with the learner. Existing quantized-RL methods are designed primarily for single-turn generation. They align the learner forward with quantized rollout or correct the current-token rollout-learner ratio, without modeling the policy history that produces each agent state. Even after quantization alignment, residual rollout-learner mismatch accumulates along the state-reaching policy history, so a current action may look locally aligned despite a mismatched history. We introduce InterQ-RL (Interaction-aware Quantized Reinforcement Learning) to correct this post-alignment mismatch. It applies bounded execution-prefix correction over the state-reaching policy history, allocates correction strength across action segments by effective support under a fixed displacement budget, and requires no additional model forward pass. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) backbones from 4B to 30B on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, with all quantized arms sharing the same rollout with 8-bit weights, activations, and KV cache (W8A8-KV8). Across four environment-backbone settings, InterQ-RL achieves the strongest quantized endpoint result, matching BF16 to within 0.7 points and exceeding it in two settings. It matches or exceeds the learning speed of alignment alone while avoiding its late performance regression.
core_methodology: Interaction-aware Quantized Reinforcement Learning (InterQ-RL) focusing on correcting execution mismatches in multi-turn agent RL
data_sources: Not applicable (evaluated on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, not financial markets)
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability; potentially useful for optimizing quantized RL execution in trading algorithms, but no direct financial market application demonstrated

title: SN-EDA: Skew-Normal Estimation of Distribution Algorithms
summary: Gaussian estimation of distribution algorithms (EDAs) converge prematurely on slopes, because truncation selection removes most of the variance along the gradient. The usual remedies enlarge the variance or shift the mean. We propose the skew-normal EDA (SN-EDA), which corrects the third moment instead. It samples from a skew-normal distribution whose skewness points along the cumulative path of the mean shifts, while the mean and covariance remain exactly the maximum-likelihood estimates. The estimation step is unchanged, and the skewness needs no control. On a linear function it raises the fraction of the variance that survives selection from 0.29 to 0.53. In a pre-registered test on 24 benchmark functions in 10, 20 and 40 dimensions the skewness, applied through a gate that the test finds dispensable, improves the Gaussian EDA significantly in five of six settings. When the population starts far from the optimum, the error, averaged logarithmically over a run, falls by one to three orders of magnitude, and the gain grows with the magnitude of the skewness as predicted. The skewness adds nothing to the anticipated mean shift, whose offspring distribution we show to be skewed already, and SN-EDA remains behind algorithms that also correct the second moment.
core_methodology: Skew-normal estimation of distribution algorithms (SN-EDA) that corrects the third moment (skewness) instead of enlarging variance or shifting mean to improve optimization performance.
data_sources: Benchmark optimization test functions (abstract mentions 24 benchmark functions in 10, 20, and 40 dimensions).
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability to trading; may have niche uses in non-convex portfolio optimization scenarios where skewness modeling is critical.

title: Online Prediction System for Proactive Autoscaling
summary: We present an online learning system for short-term time series forecasting that enables proactive autoscaling in large-scale distributed systems. Unlike traditional forecasting methods that focus on modeling seasonality and long-term trends, the system targets high-accuracy, low-latency predictions for immediate future intervals for dynamic resource management in internet-scale infrastructures. The system employs a two-stage architecture: a seasonality decomposition stage followed by a residual correction stage using lightweight linear models with engineered features. By retraining models on-the-fly for every prediction cycle, the online prediction system continuously adapts to changing demand patterns without requiring persistent model storage or feature drift monitoring. Deployed across many heterogeneous services, the system processes over 900K predictions per hour; in an offline evaluation on production traffic, its STL-based configuration reduces prediction error (MAPE) by 18.6\% relative to the previous production model. In production, the system has saved an estimated 118K servers daily.
core_methodology: Two-stage architecture involving seasonality decomposition and residual correction using lightweight linear models
data_sources: Internet-scale infrastructure demand patterns
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability to financial markets, though the online learning approach could theoretically adapt to short-term market changes
